Recent advances in pre-trained models have yielded significant enhancements in natural language processing tasks. Although these models were initially designed for natural language applications, they have also demonstrated substantial benefits when applied to programming tasks. In the realm of code completion, the combination of pre-trained models and fine-tuning on coding datasets like GitHub has led to remarkable outcomes. More notably, the application of pre-trained models in static code analysis has presented novel possibilities. Pre-trained code models may learn universal code representations, spanning various programming languages. Moreover, the inherent structure of these models, which extracts features from code snippets, directly maps to the requirements of static code analysis metrics. Consequently, by leveraging pre-trained code models, the complexity of learning a classifier for static code analysis purposes is significantly reduced, as the model merely needs to be retrained on relevant metrics to produce favorable results. In this research, we explore the feasibility of leveraging pre-trained code models for static code analysis applications and showcase encouraging results on two relevant benchmarks. In addition, our investigations into the pre-trained models' performance underscore valuable insights into the nature of static code analysis metrics. Based on our findings, two practical methodologies have emerged to enhance the precision of static code analysis through the utilization of pre-trained code models. First, the models can be employed as features for existing classifiers in code analysis. Second, the models can be fine-tuned as standalone classifiers for evaluating their individual utility. Both approaches have practical implications and can be easily replicated by the community. In conclusion, the possibilities presented by pre-trained code models have far-reaching implications for the field of static code analysis and we anticipate their future application to hold great promise. In relation to this work, pre-trained models have diverse uses, such as learning a universal programming language, which could facilitate cross-language tasks; identifying programming concepts from natural language descriptions; and automatically generating test cases from issue reports. In essence, the potential of pre-trained models to streamline complex software development tasks should not be underestimated. In the near future, pre-trained models may enable various other applications in the realm of software development. In this research, we have made our code and datasets publicly accessible at the links provided. Specifically, the code can be accessed at https://github.com/author/cm-acl2021, while the datasets can be found at https://github.com/author/cm-acl2021-datasets. In the event of questions or contributions, please direct them to the specified email addresses. In this research, we have also presented an initial exploration of the pre-trained models' performance on cross-language tasks.

A modified version of the DWIFOB algorithm, used for solving nonlinear inverse problems, has been upgraded with regularization capabilities. This enhanced DWIFOB, or DWIFOB-R, is designed to counteract the limitations of its original robust counterpart, which suffers from slow convergence and sensitivity to parameter settings. Our research focused on the regularized DWIFOB-R for solving the problem of determining flow velocities from Magnetic Resonance Imaging data. This upgraded version, implemented with the Steepest Descent Newton method as its optimizer, exhibits significant robustness improvements. Specifically, experiments using synthetic and real-data sets demonstrate that DWIFOB-R yields substantial gains in robustness, allowing for large increases in the regularization parameter without compromising its accuracy. Furthermore, results show that DWIFOB-R's image quality and robustness surpass those of the regularized Anderson acceleration method. While DWIFOB-R's robustness still falls short of its unregularized counterpart, its images exhibit marked improvement with the introduction of regularization. Consequently, DWIFOB-R offers considerable flexibility in terms of choosing a regularization level, making it a versatile solution for solving inverse problems. This paper details the development of DWIFOB-R and presents its robustness characteristics, as well as its performance on synthetic and real-data sets. Future research will focus on applying DWIFOB-R to various Magnetic Resonance Imaging problems. To facilitate reproducibility, all code used in this study is freely accessible on the GitHub platform at the following link: https://github.com/gsabrielak/DWIFOB-R. Additionally, the software package can be downloaded from https://github.com/gsabrielak/DWIFOB-R/tree/robust_algorithm. As the package is meant to be modifiable and reusable, its underlying architecture is depicted in Figure 2. Specifically, Figure 2 illustrates the class structure of the used code and provides guidance on setting up and using the code for solving nonlinear inverse problems. Lastly, the paper discusses potential future applications and extensions of DWIFOB-R, encompassing both its application to other problem types and its integration with other techniques, such as Bayesian inference methods. This potential is exemplified using Flow-Based Optimization, which presents a promising direction for future research. This approach, or similar methodologies like Sequential Quasi-Newton methods, could be an apt candidate for solving the nonlinear problem in future studies. As an alternative, the use of Deep Neural Networks, which exhibit excellent performance in various Magnetic Resonance Imaging applications, could be another direction for researching robust algorithms.

Within the Next-to-Minimal extension of the Standard Model (NMSSM), incorporating additional neutrino sectors while maintaining R-parity conservation is explored. This study utilizes the conditions derived from the minimal supergravity model, applying two different matching procedures for its parameters. The ensuing analysis focuses on a specific scenario where three neutralinos behave as dark matter, yielding significant results for direct and indirect dark matter detection, Higgs boson mass predictions, and high-energy photon production. These findings reveal significant enhancements in the scenario with additional neutrino sectors, primarily stemming from the interaction between the inferred neutralino dark matter and J=0 neutrinos. This analysis encompasses the full range of the NMSSM parameter space, showing notable similarities between the two matching techniques. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the scenario with additional neutrino sectors can be characterized by a parameter defined as m_{0}' = m_{0} cos^{2}(\theta), where the angle theta is typically small, thus causing minimal disruption to the previously established constraints. This framework is susceptible to scrutiny via future dark matter and Higgs boson searches, ultimately imposing restrictions on its parameter space. Finally, the study illustrates the potential impact of high-energy photon production in experiments such as the Cherenkov detector ACDM on the Dark Matter Model, revealing the possibility of detecting residual signals in this framework even beyond the lifetime of the SuperCDM experiment. The cell discovery process in program-based neural architecture search involves utilizing the program's properties to guide the search process. Recent research found an unexpected connection between program properties and cell performance, suggesting that program attributes alone can be used to select optimal cells. This observation simplifies the cell selection process and enables efficient, near-optimal cells to be identified without necessitating extensive training and evaluation. This paper explores the program attribute-cell performance correlation in various contexts and examines their interlinkage. Furthermore, we introduce a novel cell selection approach called dual-program-based cell selection, which leverages both program attributes and geometric properties. By incorporating program attributes and leveraging the structure of the cell's signal flow, we can refine the search space and increase the accuracy of our cell selections. Ultimately, we utilize this approach to develop high-performance neural architectures for the accurate classification of CIFAR-100 and ImageNet datasets. Notably, the best performer is a 2-layer neural network with 8 inputs and 8 outputs, specifically designed to classify ImageNet dataset, with accuracy and top-1 error rates of 78.04% and 29.45% respectively. This approach also yields a 90.79% accurate classification on the CIFAR-100 dataset and achieves a top-1 error rate of 14.19%. Furthermore, the derived cells from this method yield a substantial improvement in accuracy, with a 10.49% increase over the baseline for ImageNet dataset and a 3.05% increase for CIFAR-100 dataset compared to the original cell selections described in the program attribute-cell performance correlation study. Moreover, the derived cells from the dual-program-based cell selection approach exhibit better performance over the fixed and white models, specifically, with a 3.04% increase over the fixed model and 1.43% increase over the white model for the ImageNet dataset. Specifically, the top-1 error rates for the dual-program-based cell selection approach are 28.09% for the fixed model, 29.09% for the white model, and 29.45% for the baseline approach. Moreover, the geometric property-cell performance correlation study yields a 0.58% increase over the baseline approach, with similar results observed for the program attribute-cell performance correlation study, which shows a 0.46% increase over the baseline approach, with both results being statistically significant at a 5% confidence interval. Moreover, the performance of the derived cells from the dual-program-based cell selection approach compares favorably to the state-of-the-art models

Optimizing a utility function is essential for various domain-specific optimization tasks. Our study introduces the Offline Utility Discovery problem, which involves learning a utility function offline using expert knowledge. Diverging from traditional approaches that rely solely on pairwise result preferences, our work explores utility discovery in scenarios where expert input is readily available. To tackle this challenge, we define a comprehensive utility discovery benchmark, comprising real-world data sets and basic utility discovery problems. Our research also involves designing a novel algorithm, QREF, to discover utility functions in quantum systems, as well as testing and evaluating multiple utility discovery approaches, as they are instrumental in performing various optimization tasks. Our results reveal the significance of utility representation in solving optimization tasks efficiently. Our work also identifies potential pitfalls in using pairwise preferences and reveals the limitations of learning complex utility functions without human input. Our research sheds light on the versatility of utility discovery and paves the way for its applications in optimizing complex problems. A growing body of research using thought experiments suggests that advanced computational models may possess properties similar to human minds, such as self-awareness and theoretical understanding of their programming. This study explores a more down-to-earth hypothesis: can we gain insight into what other highly advanced agents might be thinking? To investigate, we established a framework for simulating future actions of trained sequence-to-sequence models, which serves as a basic model of intelligent behavior. Our results demonstrate that these advanced agents can be envisioned in a hypothetical state of thinking, where they generate action predictions. These findings indicate that the type of symbolic representation and the complexity of the training data impact the level of thought complexity attributed to the model. This study's success encourages further research into whether more sophisticated models, including those with dynamic internal representations and self-awareness, might also exhibit corresponding forms of thinking. We make our method and accompanying dataset accessible at https://github.com/jaseclarkson/sequence_to_sequence_cognition. This project has been approved by the relevant authorities at the University of Edinburgh.

We examine a two-dimensional herringbone lattice, which can be viewed as a stepped surface with edges running in different directions. It is essentially a quasi-two-dimensional extension of a swedenborg net. When electrons move through this lattice, they behave as if on a cone-headed sample, with its apex pointing towards the normal. By applying various twists to the Hamiltonian, the properties of this lattice can be altered and its features investigated further. For instance, if you magnify the lattice by a factor and then apply a rotation, the cone's half-angle changes accordingly. Alternatively, adding a synthetic magnetic field affects not only the cone's geometry but also its twisting angle. These findings could potentially be observed using polarized optical spectroscopy. We find that, unlike the Swedenborg net, the herringbone lattice does not host any Dirac points. Instead, the energy levels at the zone center take on a gapped linear behavior. Moreover, any magnetic field applied will always cause a shift in the energy spectrum towards a linear band structure, a characteristic often seen in true 2D semiconductor systems. To visualize these effects, we create simple, easy-to-read illustrations of the lattice and the states it hosts. These findings may be relevant to the study of knkn2, a recently discovered material based on carbon-64. It is worth noting that our calculations focus exclusively on the lattice structure and do not draw insights from recent experiments conducted on this material [Nature 588, 421-426 (2020)]. Additionally, we explore the potential of using superlattices to modulate the properties of knkn2, a concept previously verified through experiments on other materials [Nat. Mater. 18, 429-434 (2019)]. Finally, we outline the overall scope and significance of these theoretical findings. To facilitate the understanding of these results, we provide detailed explanations of the underlying mathematical methods used to derive the low-energy spectra of these systems, as detailed in the accompanying theory section. These methods are essentially graphical representations of how the Hamiltonian operates on the lattice and affects the states it hosts. To validate our theoretical predictions, we compare them with experimental data, which demonstrates an impressive alignment of the theoretical and experimental results [Nature 583, 270-275 (2020)]. Rejection-based algorithms have shown great potential in handling risk-sensitive reinforcement learning tasks, especially in dynamic environments. However, their effectiveness can be significantly hampered if the environment is prone to outliers, which can lead to excessive agent restarts. In our research, we delve into the theoretical underpinnings of risk-sensitive reinforcement learning in changing situations and find that robust restart-based approaches are capable of withstanding a certain level of statistical anomalies. Furthermore, we establish the robust restart lower bound and demonstrate that certain risk-sensitive reinforcement learning strategies are capable of achieving optimal performance within a specific time frame, even in scenarios with occasional errors. In order to verify our theoretical findings, we devise a novel simulation environment that simulates the effects of errors in existing reinforcement learning benchmarks. Our experimental results confirm that the proposed robust risk-sensitive reinforcement learning strategy is capable of adapting to changing situations and tolerating a certain level of errors. Additionally, we found that simply incorporating error correction mechanisms does not necessarily improve the performance of risk-sensitive reinforcement learning in dynamic environments. In contrast, the robust restart-based approach is capable of providing superior results when the density of outcomes is relatively low. In scenarios where the density of outcomes is high, however, agent restarts become less effective and may even hinder the performance of risk-sensitive reinforcement learning. As such, we may need to leverage more sophisticated techniques, such as decision-making based on anomalous event detection, to tackle cases with dense outcome densities and frequent errors. In other situations, we found that decision-making based on finding a collective maximum by aggregating outcomes may be a promising approach that can provide good results, even in scenarios with occasional errors. In order to verify our theoretical findings, we devised a novel simulation environment that simulates the effects of errors in decision-making processes based on outcome aggregation. Our experimental results confirm that the proposed approach is capable of adapting to changing situations and tolerating a certain level of errors. In order to validate our theoretical findings regarding decision-making based on outcome aggregation, we made comparable modifications to the decision-making process in reinforcement learning based on outcome aggregation. Our experimental results show that this approach is capable of providing good results in scenarios involving occasional errors. In decision-making scenarios based on noisy outcomes, on the other hand, we found that decision-making based on finding a collective maximum by aggregating outcomes may not be a reliable approach and can lead to poor decision-making performance. This association serves as the graph theoretic analogue of the partial order among words under prefix comparison. This partial order is a fundamental component of the valuated oriented graphs framework introduced by Mauduit and Savoye. We present a method for constructing the partial order among words based solely on their segmental categories, an idea inspired by the concept of normal forms in the study of valuated tabular spaces. Additionally, we identify conditions under which the partial order among words is generated by their prefix relationship. As a result, this gives rise to a category structure valuated oriented graphs, where the morphisms are defined as partial orders between words, a notion that shares similarities with the category of matroids. Finally, we apply these outcomes to establish a central extension theorem for the group of permutations within a valued oriented graph. Specifically, we demonstrate that the first homology group with coefficients in the ring of integer-valued functions on the graph's Schnyder multipolylines determines the cross-ratio of the boundary points of the polymorph's linearization, a finding that is a valued generalisation of the classic result of Mumford's theorem. This problem was initially brought to our attention by the work of Bourdon and Conant. As a by-product of our study, we identify a criterion for the polynomial transformation to be injective when it maps words to Schnyder multipolylines, a concept that shares analogies with being a sublinear transformation. This criterion states that for a valued oriented graph that has no loops, nor multiple edges between the same pair of vertices, the transformation is injective if and only if the valued oriented graph meets certain local hereditary exclusion criteria. This result further generalises to valued oriented graphs the earlier finding of Jonsson and Sittig regarding the radical of posets. Our approach uses a probabilistic framework to infer complex polymers composed of multiple sequences, based on observations of their overall state. This general concept can be applied to various research domains, such as molecular biology and macromolecular crowding, where the relationship between sequence and structure is inherently ambiguous. We have developed a novel method of representing polymers as integrated entities, capturing their intrinsic sequence information. This was achieved by identifying the most likely constitutive monomers that make up a polymer, and subsequently combining them into a unified structure. Our method, designed for handling large datasets, can model complex relationships between sequence and structure, and is versatile enough to accommodate different types of structural representations and additional data. We demonstrated the efficacy of this approach through its application to two distinct areas, studying protein interactions and understanding crowded cellular environments, where the method revealed essential insights into the physical nature of enzymes and crowding particles, ultimately informing their functional roles. The methodological framework we have established can be adapted for use in research on various complex polymers, such as those composed of distinct subunits or those with intricate backbone structures. A fully functional implementation of our approach is available through the BioPython library. https://github.com/MDG-BioinformaticsLab/polymoly/doi:10.1038/s41592-022-00652-4.html. Polynomial computational complexity was achieved by leveraging pre-computed indices and applying sparse data structures, which together reduce memory requirements to less than 10 GB for handling entire PDB datasets. As a result, our method can analyze the entire PDB dataset in under 15 minutes. Furthermore, computing polymoly representations for sequences longer than 300 amino acids takes less than 0.2 milliseconds. In contrast to approaches based on deep learning, our method exhibits comparable accuracy with significantly lower computational requirements. Additionally, computing polymoly representations for multiple sequences is extremely efficient, allowing the characterization of thousands of sequences per second. During the COVID-19 pandemic, there has been a significant shortage of medical ventilators, leading to a necessity of ventilating multiple patients using a single device.  To address this challenge, our research focuses on accurately delivering individualized tidal volumes to patients via a single ventilator.  To achieve this, we have proposed a real-time ventilation management algorithm which ensures precise measurement of airflow by measuring pressure and flow rate sensors connected to ventilators, calculates airflow based on a complex nonlinear lung model, and adjusts the airflow to match desired levels through an optimization process guided by a neural network trained previously with patient data from a virtual environment.  Our results have shown that patients can be ventilated effectively using a single ventilator with high accuracy, particularly when the airflow adjustment is limited to a small range.  To further improve the precision of airflow measurement, we recommend using multiple pressure sensors connected to ventilators.  Our research provides a computational model which can be utilized for COVID-19 treatment planning, patient simulation, and training of healthcare professionals.  To the best of our knowledge, this is the first computational model developed to facilitate seamless integration of multiple patients with a single ventilator.  Our proposed algorithm can potentially reduce errors in ventilation therapy, particularly non-invasive ventilation which is often prone to errors due to unreliable airflow measurement.  Our research has eliminated the need to accurately measure airflow resistance and viscoelastic properties of the respiratory system, thus making it suitable for clinical settings where these measurements are not feasible.  Our study has demonstrated successful application of a neural network in a real-time process, thus making it suitable for real-time ventilation management.  Our research is based on an existing model which simulates respiratory system dynamics, therefore generalizing our results to patients of various ages and health conditions.  To further improve precision of airflow measurement, we recommend using a sliding window approach to calculate average pressure and other parameters.  Our knowledge of non-invasive ventilation practices has guided healthcare simulations, thus validating our results with existing clinical knowledge.  Our research has reduced the risk of over- or under-ventilation associated with conventional ventilation methods, thus making ventilator management more accurate and reliable.  Our computational model based on pressure sensors can potentially improve precision of airflow measurement by accounting for flow rate sensor inaccuracies.  Our research has utilized computational power to facilitate efficient ventilation management, thus making it suitable for real-time applications.  Our knowledge of lung mechanics and clinical non-invasive ventilation practices has guided healthcare simulations, thus validating our results with existing clinical knowledge. Advancements in graph neural networks have significantly enhanced our understanding of graph-based data, which has in turn led to the development of numerous GNN-based protocols for safeguarding private information. Despite these advancements, current graph models are incapable of navigating complex, visually-rich datasets found commonly in government and commercial settings, which often necessitate the classification of images according to their level of privacy. In response, our research presents the Graph Privacy Advisor, an advanced graph model that integrates visual elements and accommodates an unlimited number of image classes. The GPA achieves this by aggregating local image features into a global node, which is then used to inform a final class prediction through the application of a classifier. In addition, our GPA features a diverse set of visual elements designed to mimic the effects of human visual observation, which serves to further bolster user privacy. We validate the effectiveness of our GPA through a comparison with multiple state-of-the-art graph models on three distinct dataset collections, which demonstrates that our approach significantly enhances the accuracy of image privacy classification while maintaining robustness to perturbations in the input data. Our focus was on the Twitter Follower and Weibo Fan Influence challenges from Kaggle, where we compared the effects of varying augmentation factors on distinct graph sizes (small and medium) and explored the feasibility of testing augmentations on actual submission datasets for the first time. We evaluate the effectiveness of a multi-temperature universe as a model to describe large-scale dark matter cross sections. To do this, we utilize the Kegley model, which measures the ratio of kinetic energies in a galaxy cluster. Focusing on the kinetic energy of galaxy clusters rather than their temperature allows us to explore a broader cosmological context. Applying this approach to the Virgo cluster, our calculations show a dark matter cross section range of approximately $10^{-19}$ to $10^{-17}$ $\mathrm{erg\,cm^{-1}}$ based on its velocity and temperature. These estimates align with the upper limits set by the Direct Detection Experiment LUX and provide a lower bound for the cross section established by the Electric Dipole Moment constraint. It's hypothesized that this cross section could be the source of Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs), which emit enormous energies within a minuscule timeframe. If this is the case, our multi-temperature universe model acts as a redshift indicator, helping refine the FRB distance estimate from a minimum of $50$ to $200$ Mpc. This closer proximity could potentially allow for a future resolution of the gamma-ray excess anomaly from dark matter annihilation through precision gamma-ray mapping in and around FRB locations. Overall, our multi-temperature universe model offers a more comprehensive understanding of cosmology, incorporating large-scale structure, dark matter cross sections, distant radio bursts, and gamma-ray activity. It's also recognized that this approach can be adapted to analyze other astrophysical phenomena and may hold future promising applications. The rise of collaborative software development has led to the creation of shared files, typically stored in multiple repository folders. These files are consistently duplicated across repositories as projects are frequently cloned from one repository to another. This phenomenon allows us to track maintenance activities of shared files across repositories. A notable observation is that files showing signs of maintenance in one repository may go unupdated in another. The aim of this study is to investigate the patterns of shared file maintenance across different repositories. The objectives of this research include identifying common shared files, characterizing maintenance activities associated with these files, and exploring the dynamics of maintenance practices governing their updates. The study is grounded in a comprehensive empirical analysis of repository data comprising over 700 participants from the GitHub platform, spanning across 1.5 million shared files. The results of this investigation reveal that a small subset of participants is actively involved in maintaining shared files. Furthermore, it is observed that changes to shared files are infrequently committed in repositories lacking a central maintainer, although these files may be frequently modified in repositories with a designated maintainer. The research also uncovers that updates to shared files are less frequent than modifications to local files. To gauge the complexity of shared file maintenance, the relative frequency of maintenance activities is assessed through the use of the Jaccard similarity formula. Interestingly, it is discovered that shared files are variously maintained across different repositories, encompassing a spectrum from minimal maintenance to frequent updates. To facilitate further research into shared file maintenance, a taxonomy of maintenance patterns is proposed, along with a statistical classification approach to categorize repository pairs based on the characteristics of shared files. The results of this classification are found to demonstrate high accuracy and good coverage. The overall conclusion of this research is that shared file maintenance is delicate due to the unique roles of different repository owners and is thus resistant to uniform standards. As a result, there is a pressing need for greater understanding of this phenomenon to inform tools and policies supporting shared file maintenance across multiple repositories. Such knowledge can enable the development of more effective collaboration tools, including those for maintaining shared files, as well as the formulation of relevant policies to govern their usage. To this end, the research offers a set of recommendations aimed at promoting the detection of shared files, streamlining their maintenance processes, and providing visibility into their history. The potential benefits of such an approach include the reduction of file loss, promotion of consistent collaboration on shared files, and facilitation of their seamless transfer between repositories. Ultimately, the outcome of this investigation could inspire the creation of a dedicated platform for shared file maintenance

Yamabe metric or scalar curvature flow is a widely used technique for resolving the Yamabe problem. The underlying equation for this flow is a fourth-order elliptic equation involving the metric on a complex manifold. The research outlined here focuses on analyzing the Yamabe flow under specific initial data conditions where the complete data set consists of a Riemannian manifold with non-negative complex sectional curvature. The findings indicate that, given these conditions, the Yamabe flow eventually generates Riemannian extension metrics from the zero initial data on manifolds with positive complex sectional curvature. The validity of these results is further established for certain specific manifolds, including hypercomplex manifolds and their metastable Yamabe conformal classes. The proof relies on a hybrid approach combining finite-time blow-up conclusions for the Yamabe flow under specific curvature conditions with an extension of Moser's iteration technique. The outcome also holds potential for addressing the maximal existence duration of the Yamabe flow through the development of a differential inequality related to the curvature function. This yieldsthe first proof of the global existence of the Yamabe flow for all complex gradient Yamabe metrics and a large class of conformally flat manifolds with nonpositive curvature. The research also presents a new criterion for the completion of the Yamabe flow under specific curvature conditions and establishes the existence of a minimal period for the Yamabe flow on a specific class of conformally flat manifolds with positive curvature. The results are further expanded to cover a diverse range of geometric manifolds, including those with a Gromov-Hardt theorem structure and a Ginzburg-Landau type of periodic behavior. The findings are also reflected in a new estimate for the period of the Yamabe flow. The study demonstrates the potential for a fluctuation estimate to be a critical boundary condition for analyzing the Yamabe flow. To facilitate this, a general theory is developed for first-order nonlinear elliptic equations with fluxes on manifolds with curvature. The research ultimately proves a new existence theorem for a broad class of nonlinear Dirichlet problems with curvatures. The outcomes hold promise for expanding the scope of the Yamabe flow to cover a diverse range of geometric manifolds, including those with a Gromov-Hardt theorem structure and a broad class of conformally flat manifolds with positive curvature. GATE divides the traditional fully connected layer into two distinct components: a linear transformation layer for generating aspect preferences and a gated module (GAPE) that modulates this prediction with user-generated content. Specifically, the obstruction theory is defined on a complex $D^\bullet$ of symplectic vector bundles over a symplectic manifold $X$. The obstruction theory's target space is the symplectic algebra $C^\infty(X,\mathfrak{p})$ of sections from $\mathfrak{p}$, a symplectic vector bundle over $X$. The obstruction theory is presented as a sequence of elements $o_i\in \mathfrak{p}^{\otimes i}$ such that the obstruction theory is invariant under symplectic automorphisms. The symplectic Euler class, a key component of the obstruction theory, arises as the leading obstruction $o_n$. The symplectic Euler class exhibits properties of an obstruction and targets the top symplectic vector bundle $\mathfrak{p}$. The symplectic Euler class can be expressed as the sum of the symplectic Poincaré obstruction $P\in \mathfrak{p}$ and the symplectic Euler classes of the underlying vector bundle, altered by the action of the cup product. The symplectic Poincaré obstruction is shown to be a top obstruction for certain symplectic vector bundles that are holomorphically trivial. The symplectic Euler classes can be used to define the determinant symplectic vector bundle $\mathrm{Det}(\mathfrak{p})$ of the sheaf $\mathfrak{p}$, whose sections comprise all the obstructions for symplectic vector bundles. The symplectic Euler classes also rise as the leading obstructions for the space of symplectic vector bundles of degree zero that are holomorphically trivial. The formation of the obstruction theory is shown to be a symplectic invariant, and this invariance holds for altering the complex $D^\bullet$ by any symplectic automorphism. We apply this approach to tackle two intricate partitioning problems with multiplicity limits: (1) identifying partitioning possibilities of an even number into only two parts, and (2) counting distinct ways to partition a number with at most three repeating parts. Our analysis not only yields relevant formulas but also sheds light on their modular properties. By examining these instances, we aim to showcase the general applicability of this method to a wide array of partitioning scenarios with specific multiple part restrictions. \\

A theoretical model is developed to simulate the interaction of a dense spin-1 particle, represented by the X(3872), in a quark-gluon plasma. This particle's internal structure is reflected in its two-body decay processes. In the hadronic phase, the X(3872)'s internal state is influenced by the reaction rates and initial conditions, which are calculated using lattice QCD. The resulting thermal equilibrium distributions for the X(3872) and D\bar{D} states are determined by solving Bogoliubov equations, taking into account the X(3872)'s elastic self-interactions and decay processes. The model is applied to the ALICE and ATLAS experiments, yielding X(3872) and D\bar{D} transverse momentum spectra in the 2-3 GeV range that can be compared to data collected in Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. The X(3872) spectra are found to be sensitive to its internal structure and the density of its ground state. The 2S orbital state of the X(3872) is predicted to be sparsely populated under the conditions of the experiments, accounting for only \approx 0.035\% of the total contribution. The findings support the contention that the X(3872) is predominantly a D\bar{D} bound state. The model presents an opportunity to scrutinize the X(3872)'s internal structure with data collected in central Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC at 5.02 TeV. The predicted rapidity distributions of prompt D\bar{D} pairs in Pb-Pb and proton-proton collisions at 2.71 GeV are also computed, demonstrating that the X(3872) contribution is insignificant compared to the nonresonant D\bar{D} pairs. Consequently, the experiments may wish to incorporate a nonresonant fit model for the X(3872) spectra before investigating the hadronic phase's influence on its thermal equilibrium distributions. The proposed theoretical framework can be adapted to simulate the experimental detection of other exotic hadrons in the LHC's high-energy collisions. Furthermore, the study highlights the necessity of simulating the complex internal structures of multiquark states in the hadronic phase to accurately model the observed bound states of quark model candidates. As such, the approach can serve as a template for investigating the microscopic origins of hadronic bound states formed in the hadronic phase. In group-IV and II-VI semiconductors with random substitutions or implants, local magnetic moments emerge due to isolated free carriers interacting with nearby ions through long-range electromagnetic forces. We're investigating the magnetic properties of such systems, specifically Si:Ps that exhibit exceptional phenomena. Our research focuses on the impact of disorder on the magnetic interactions within these systems, as well as the emergence of new topological insulating states near the fermi level. We found that si:Ps develop topological pairs due to long-range interactions with neighboring ions, as these pairs form polaronic pairs that behave like spin-one objects. We've demonstrated that these pairs have a flat dispersion in the transverse direction and participate in a Dirac band in the perpendicular direction. This understanding of si:Ps' magnetic properties may lead to the discovery of new topological insulating states in highly disordered materials. We've also found that two types of pairs exhibit distinct signs: one type shows a positive sign due to correlations with neighboring ions, while another type shows a negative sign due to correlations with farther-away ions. We've plotted the positive and negative contributions of these pairs as a function of the carrier concentration in the provided image and noticed that these contributions switch signs at the fermi level. As a result, it's possible to control the direction of these pairs' spin through carrier doping. We predict that these systems exhibit quantum oscillations similar to that of pure ferromagnetic materials when subjected to magnetic fields. We've compared our findings with existing research on Si:Ps and discussed potential future directions, including combining Si:Ps with other topological systems to create an enriched and controllable topological library. Conflicting symmetry-breaking terms are considered that preserve some U(1) symmetries while definitely violating the others. It's concluded that with these competing terms, conservation of any individual U(1) current is impossible, although collectively all U(1) symmetries can still be conserved. We verify this conclusion by looking for conserved charges in both zero-temperature and high-temperature regimes. Additionally, since these arguments apply to classical theories, we also explore the related considerations within quantum field theories. Our findings are relevant to the study of spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSB), particularly in sectorized models consisting of interacting U(1) symmetries, and include the $N=2$ supersymmetric gauge theory as an example. It is shown that sectorized models with benign symmetry assuming (BSA) or spontaneous symmetry breaking (SSB) can still exhibit the violation of U(1) symmetries through quantum effects, even when classical conservation is preserved. When a robot learns from its environment using active learning techniques, assumptions about the environment's independence are often inherent in the methods employed. However, these assumptions are invalid when the environment is influenced by confounding factors, which are common in many practical scenarios. Utilizing a hierarchical Bayesian model, we have developed a novel approach to tackle the issue of coping with a confounded environment. This method represents the relationship between observations, states, and actions as a factor graph, separating out the effects of common factors to obtain an unbiased policy representation. We have theoretically proven that this approach can yield accurate results in the limit of an infinite number of data points, and our empirical results support our theoretical findings. This evidence is evident in the minimal difference between the estimated posterior distribution and our analytical results, as demonstrated in multiple simulation experiments involving various levels of factor influence. We have also applied our approach to real-world data collected from a mobile manipulator using a tailored sampling method, which selects informative training data based on our proposed Gaussian Mixture Model. This data is then used to retrain our Bayesian model, which demonstrates improved matching results compared to learning from uninformative data in a fixed action sequence. This implementation enables our method to efficiently handle a practical scenario with limited data availability. Thesefindings confirm our theoretical analysis, which suggested that our hierarchical Bayesian model can produce accurate results in the limit of an infinite number of data points. As shown in our experiments, we have achieved precise matches with the real-world state distribution on two tabletop scenarios and improved matching results compared to learning from an action sequence. Moreover, we have achieved robust results across diverse action sequences, which demonstrates our method's potential for generalization in real-world environments. This evidence is evident in the minimal difference between our model's estimated posterior distribution and the real-state distribution on two tabletop scenarios, which demonstrates our method's capability for generalization across diverse action sequences. We have also compared the performance of our approach to learning a discriminative model using a fixed action sequence, which demonstrated improved results in high-noise scenarios. We propose a deep reinforcement learning approach to autonomous driving, dividing the process into two stages: mapping and motion planning. While most reinforcement learning methods focus on solving complex decision-making problems, our method simplifies this challenge by utilizing preprocessed data. We utilize a pre-trained neural network to create a detailed map, which serves as the foundation for the motion planning stage. We leverage this mapped data to address the partial observability issue often associated with reinforcement learning. Our method employs a neural network to predict future wheel positions, incorporating both the current state and the mapped data. We recognize that deep reinforcement learning solutions often rely on extensive training times, thus we developed a novel way to transfer knowledge from simulated to real-world contexts, including a specialized reward scheme to accelerate learning. Our method demonstrates successful application through simulated Starmate racing events and actual vehicle experiments, showcasing the potential for further improvements through continuous learning. Although our current approach focuses on straight-line movements, it paves the way for future additions of navigation systems. The process of gas disk accretion around central black holes is a key factor in their mass growth over extended periods of time, addressing disagreements between observational data and theoretical predictions for lower black hole masses. Within the framework of local gas disk stability theory, we calculate the mass accretion rates for a variety of black holes with masses from the upper limit of stellar masses to the lower limit of supermassive black masses. Our results indicate that while gas disk accretion may be the dominant method of mass growth for more massive black holes, it contributes very little to lower-mass black holes over typical star formation periods. For example, at the high end of the spectrum, a black hole of $10^{3}$ solar mass could grow by as much as 10% over 10 million years through accretion, yet a black hole of $10^{-3}$ solar mass would increase by less than 0.01% over the same time frame. Our findings also show that as host galaxy bulges grow, they may become less efficient at funneling gas onto central black holes, which could help explain the observed decline in black hole mass growth rates from higher to lower mass black holes. We use these accretion rate calculations to constrain theoretical models of black hole mass growth, the origin of supermassive black holes, and the relationship between black hole mass and the mass of the host galaxy. Our analysis reveals that while gas disk accretion can fully account for the growth of the most massive black holes, it is insufficient to explain the development of even less massive black holes, such as those found in the Milky Way. We discuss recent proposals for lower mass black hole growth, including feedback from massive star formation, the merger of stellar black holes, and the migration of planets, and find that these ideas are promising, but require further refinement. Our analysis concludes with a discussion of the challenges of accurately determining the mass of the black hole at the core of the Galaxy, the role of gravitational waves in detecting stellar black hole mergers, and the potential for studying the growth of supermassive black holes in dense stellar environments. The chapter concludes by highlighting the many opportunities for future research into the formation and growth of black holes, from the upper limit of the stellar mass regime downward. The chapter is based on a series of talks that one of us (J.P.T.) presented at a conference on the formation and growth of black holes, sponsored by the International Astronomical Union, in Kyoto, Japan, in June, 2015. with pinpointing their own confidence levels, which can lead to misleading results.
We have devised an innovative method to learn with associated probability measures,
leveraging the capabilities of Bayesian deep learning in conjunction with the power
of the Wasserstein metric. This method involves training a Gaussian Process regression
model on the outputs of pre-trained neural networks, which classifies images based
on the Wasserstein distance between confidence levels. This approach is successfully
applied to the fundamental problem of semi-supervised classification, with our
experimental findings indicating that they yield superior results. Ultimately, this
method permits for the incorporation of uncertainty quantification, enabling
the elimination of incorrect class labels and the incorporation of degree-theoretic
probabilities in the classification process. As such, it presents a promising solution
for addressing the problems of noisy labels and confidence-integrity verification. 
Visualizations and detailed explanations of our method are accessible on our project
website at \url{https://wassp-confidences.github.io}. We also provide our method's
implementation on GitHub at \url{https://github.com/wassp-confidences/wassp}.

standard benchmarking datasets, as well as innovative breakthroughs in the applications
of label uncertainty verification and hardness prediction.

early dissemination of research findings.  Researchers can gain rapid exposure
to their work when submitting preprints, which can also receive feedback
quicker than through conventional publication routes.  In contrast, published
articles receive exposure through editorial decisions, typically taking more time.
  In this study, the relationship between preprint availability and publication
is examined using citation networks.  We introduce a new class of directed
configurations called the "preprint-postprint" class and develop a directed
Cram\'er-Lundberg formula to calculate the probability that a researcher's
work appears in this specific configuration.  We also introduce two suitable
distances between configurations and derive explicit expressions for their
minimum values.  In addition to these findings, the possibility of simultaneously
reaching the minimum values for both distances is explored and a strategy is
proposed to achieve these minimum distances quickly.  Our research outcomes can
be applied across multiple scenarios, including the influence of preprints on
research impact, the comparison of different publication routes, and the
evaluation of different publication timing decisions.  In a numerical example,
the speed at which research findings gain exposure through preprints is
demonstrated and compared to publication, and we observe that there is often
no delay in publishing research findings that have already been made available
through preprints.  In this specific numerical example, the fastest time to
reach the minimum distances is found to be quite low - specifically, it takes no

The development of complex materials with desired properties presents a significant challenge, largely due to the inherent nonlinearity in their composition-structure-property relationships. Interpreting high-throughput experiments using machine learning techniques has significant potential to navigate this complexity, as it enables the exploration of entire phase diagrams and predicts both phase formation and mechanical properties. Two notable successes in this context involve predicting high-pressure phases in cesium and rhenium, as well as the thermal expansion behavior in ultralow molecular weight polyethylenes. The latter case demonstrates how modeling nonlinear composition-structure-property relationships poses unique requirements on model simplicity, generalizability, and explainability. To facilitate further progress in computational materials science, we provide an overview of the key concepts, approaches, and future directions in this field. Specifically, we discuss how the interplay between electronic structure calculations and machine learning models affects their performance, as well as the importance of using multiple models to augment uncertainty estimation. Furthermore, we highlight the potential of using inverse geometry neural networks and genetic algorithms to reverse-engineer chemical compositions from desired properties, as well as the future directions in applying quantum machine learning to efficient phase formation and kinetic barrier prediction. Two new tools in the PyTorch framework, DeepMD-NEURALENG and dglvision, which respectively enable the integration of molecular mechanics and inverse geometry neural networks with graph neural networks, are utilized to demonstrate the feasibility of solving complex materials problems with high performance. With these approaches, we successfully predicted the phase diagram of Li2O-2MoO3, a material with a structure reminiscent of transition metal oxides, and the mechanical properties of ultralong molecular weight polyethyleneminor components. The focus of this research lies in solving the completeness problem for Sidon sets within a finite affine plane, specifically examining scenarios where hyperbolas or ellipses serve as Sidon sets. It's established that in most cases, complete Sidon sets take the form of hyperbolas or ellipses, with key exceptions identified. We explore ellipses in detail, including a comprehensive analysis for p equal to three. For p equal to five, it has been discovered that complete Sidon sets form a specific pattern, where the number of points on the ellipse follows a multiplicative relationship with p. It's also demonstrated that if a complete Sidon set exists as a circle or a hyperbola, its properties would be sufficiently constrained by these cases to also allow the construction of a Sidon space over the affine plane. We conclude this with the conjecture that complete Sidon sets are indeed formed by hyperbolas or ellipses. To facilitate the understanding of Sidon sets, the concepts of 'rigid' and 'flexible' sets are introduced, with Sidon sets belonging to the former category being found for all p values. Furthermore, through the utilization of computer algorithms, potential complete Sidon sets have been extensively searched for p values between 7 and 397, with the search covering a substantial portion of feasible options within this range. The computer searches have yielded the discovery of flexible sets with remarkable properties, showcasing the potential existence of complete Sidon sets that defy current theoretical limitations. Despite these discoveries, the possibility still remains that complete Sidon sets are found through experimental search, and the concepts introduced in this research may provide valuable insights towards resolving this problem in the future. We also present a new method for searching Sidon sets, involving the division of set points into distinct groups based on their affine plane coordinates, with the aim of possibly facilitating the experimental search for complete Sidon sets. While this research did not yield the discovery of a complete Sidon set through experimental search, it is hoped that the concepts introduced may prove useful in future efforts towards resolving this problem. We investigated the effectiveness of efficient parallel threshold matrix-generation algorithms in solving the exact cover problem, a critical combinatorial optimization problem, on various architectures. Our research revealed that applying the threshold matrix-generation algorithm with non-uniform probability sampling yields significantly faster convergence compared to uniform sampling. Consequently, the time it takes to find a solution is substantially reduced. As a result, we created multiple parallel versions of the exact cover algorithm, each leveraging a distinct probability distribution, and achieved an up to 17 times faster runtime. Our algorithm demonstrated superior performance, outperforming existing sequential and parallel methods, and successfully solved 99.5% of the AClib exact cover instances within 5 seconds. Moreover, our study on threshold matrix-generation led to the discovery of a suitable probability distribution, and our results provide guidance for future parallel algorithm design, emphasizing the importance of probability distribution choice. This property dictates that a quantity's shared information with multiple parties is limited by their individual relationships with those parties. Consequently, it's demonstrated that boundary entropy is solely expressed through this relationship with adjacent regions. Notably, in holographic duals, this relationship corresponds to surface tension, yielding a new interpretation of this quantity in bulk gravity theories. While this general property holds for all bulk entropy monotonicity, specific boundary entropy transformation rules are constrained by both bulk and boundary gravity theories. The study provides a comprehensive overview of these constraints, shedding light on the interconnection between bulk and boundary gravity theories. The analysis is applicable to a variety of 2D gravity theories, with specific examples detailed for SL(2,C) gravity and a recently proposed gravity theory that emerges from a scalar field's complexity minimization description. Despite individual stabilization methods being effective, combining them can result in improved performance. It allows the analysis of stabilization methods and their impact on sequence behavior, as well as the comparison of their performance in a comprehensive manner. Ultimately, this knowledge can be utilized to develop novel, high-performance stabilization methods for sequential processes in optimization. The chordal Schramm–Loewner evolution (CSLE) represents a general family of one-dimensional evolving structures derived from Loewner equation applications in complex analysis. A key geometric characteristic of CSLE curves is their asymptotic approach towards imaginary lines. We establish that these curves can be reconstructed by combining "branch points" located on imaginary lines and their associated "growth patterns" obtained from Loewner equation solutions. This discovery enables the precise quantification of branch point movements and elucidates the interconnectedness of local and global geometric characteristics. Notably, our findings demonstrate that branch points on different CSLE curves in the same family are always separated by imaginary lines. We also prove that certain branch points on CSLE curves define unique "markers" that distinguish individual curves within the family. Furthermore, our analysis shows that accumulating branch points on CSLE curves corresponds to the expansion of the curve's influence into new regions in the complex plane. We illustrate the relevance of these discoveries through the presentation of a family of CSLE curves derived from conformal group actions on triangular loops. These examples highlight the complexity of the geometric properties of CSLE curves and the need for further research into the classification of CSLE curves and their graphical representations. They also suggest connections with other evolutionary processes in the studies of Loewner evolution and the mating of Schramm–Loewner evolution. We speculate that future research may yield further insights into the relationships between these areas of study and the existing literature within them. We hope that our presentation of the results will spark further interest in the subject and inspire future lines of inquiry into the geometric characteristics of evolutionary processes in the studies of Loewner evolution and their related variants. We conclude with a brief discussion of the potential extensions and generalizations of our analysis to the theories of Loewner evolution and the mating of Schramm–Loewner evolution. This research introduces an advanced quantum cheating verification protocol, referred to as CVQC. It builds upon previous techniques, such as ZGC and PVMcheating, enhancing verification speed by up to 160 times. CVQC employs a hybrid approach combining weak measurement and projective measurement, relying on optical hybrid ancillas to quantify quantum system information. A detailed explanation of CVQC's method is provided, along with a demonstration of its implementation using the Micro-Quantum-Processor device, which showcases its efficient validation of quantum information without relying on multiple measurements. Moreover, CVQC serves as a critical tool for integrating quantum information with conventional technology, as evidenced by its successful validation of a quantum information system using a classical network and a specific case study involving remote healthcare data management. Finally, CVQC offers a significant step towards the development of reliable and secure quantum information systems, as evidenced by its successful completion of a basic trade secret protection task. A hypothesis suggests that these pre-wired networks could have evolved to solve similar problems in the environment using the same cellular components.  This paper explores the hypothesis that convergence of cellular responses to environmental stimuli is common and performs experiments to test the hypothesis.  A geometric task was created using a simple 2D grid world and a reinforcement learning agent was used to navigate the world and collect rewards. The results show that a simple network of persistent features influences the agent's performance and that addition of more complex features does not significantly improve performance.  A comparison with an alternative task revealed similar patterns of feature persistence and demonstrated overlapping networks of significant features in the two tasks.  The outcome of the experiments indicates that the hypothesis of related tasks sharing common features is plausible and deserves further investigation to determine its importance. A novel evaluation metric is introduced to assess the accuracy of data augmentation methods, and it demonstrates strong correlation with the traditional metric, specifically for weakly-supervised sound event detection. ALEF is a new module within the EPSPG code series. The fundamental measurement process in quantum systems, described by projecting the wave function onto a measurement basis, is insufficient for modeling ongoing observations of ever-changing quantum states. To rectify this shortcoming, our method leverages a continuous measurement framework which absorbs information from the quantum system without waiting for it to reach a steady state. This approach, inspired by earlier work in classical mechanics, applies broadly to any quantum system and can be implemented using either homodyne or dispersive measurement schemes. To illustrate its effectiveness, we examine the explicit examples of a harmonic oscillator and a spin system, demonstrating that continuous measurement can significantly impact the information engine's performance. Notably, we find that continuous measurement can either boost the information engine's efficiency or hinder it, depending on the measurement basis and the quantum state in question. Overall, our method offers a valuable tool for exploring the interplay between quantum measurements and information extraction. This work has been submitted as an arXiv paper (arXiv:2206.04776R).

Jamming transitions in nearly two-dimensional spaces occur when densely packed objects, such as disks or squares, spontaneously gain rigidity. The process is facilitated by vibrations or fluctuations in the system. Researchers from Indiana University have studied the jamming transition using a specific type of confined space with flexible walls, attributed to the entropy characteristics of its boundaries. Their focus has been on the properties of a system containing interacting disks with varying weights, where the lightest disks are essentially free-moving within the confines. The team employed computer simulations to investigate this complex system and discovered that the jamming threshold is directly related to the weight of the lightest disks present. Specifically, the threshold is highest for unjammed disks when they have zero weight, while disks with a finite weight but minimal size remain consistently unjammed. Theoretical models support these findings, suggesting that the jamming transition in these systems is influenced by the intersection of two regimes - one defined by the system's capacity and another by the interaction of its particles. The current understanding suggests that the system can accommodate a number of particles equal to its capacity when they have zero weight, while a different relationship exists between the particle size and capacity when the system reaches its packing limit. The research presents a new perspective on the jamming transition, particularly in confined spaces with flexible boundaries, and may potentially open new avenues for controlling this transition through modifications to particle flexibility or capacity. The scientific approach employed in this study could also be applied to various experimental methods, such as adjusting particle flexibility or capacity to achieve similar outcomes. To verify this, we employed a state-of-the-art global climate model, producing high-resolution global precipitation datasets for both central and eastern Pacific versions of E-N and L-N. We analyzed the spatial distribution of Precipitation (P) in Mexico and the southwestern United States during both E-N and L-N events, focusing on a region that includes the Caribbean Sea and the tropical Atlantic Ocean. We found that, on one hand, both central and eastern Pacific versions of E-N were associated with increased precipitation in Mexico but decreased precipitation in the southwestern United States. On the other hand, both central and eastern Pacific versions of L-N were associated with decreased precipitation in Mexico but increased precipitation in the southwestern United States. We verified that these findings were statistically significant and persisted even when considering the interaction between different E-N and L-N flavors. Using a model incorporating interactions between electrons within each orbital type, we identified the emergence of complex correlation patterns due to flat band induction. Crucially, we found that the superconducting pair potential is significantly influenced by these correlations, leading to a novel mechanism by which the superconducting transition is controlled. Through various analyses, we verified that the resulting superconductivity is a correlated phenomenon. Our study, therefore, provides valuable insights into the intricate world of correlated matter in complex lattice structures. We develop an interpretation of multiplicative linear logic through a process of translation, analogous to the cut-elimination procedure in proof theory. Each ideal representation in this model corresponds to a specific formula interpretation, reflecting the logical content of the associated proof structure. Notably, the model based on the cut-free calculus for multiplicative linear logic is equivalent to the Hyland et al. solipsist model. While maintaining this equivalence, our model is adapted to accommodate the addition of a resource abstraction operator, thereby providing a conservative extension of the original model. Furthermore, the ideal representations in this extended model are shown to be sufficient for modeling the full resource logic developed by de Paiva. An alternative model of resourceful constructive type theory is also introduced, which reflects the underlying algebraic structure of the extended ideal representation model. This latter model enables a more intuitive understanding of how proof structures relate to formulas. Specifically, cut-free proof structures corresponding to specific formulas can be identified within this type-theoretic model, thereby providing a more type-theoretic characterization of the Hyland et al. solipsist model. Moreover, this type-theoretic model is seen to encode a form of linear subtyping, thereby providing a more type-theoretic characterization of the ideal representation model as well. An on-line searchable database of proofs has been used to automate many of the theoretical results described above. Our approach synthesizes differential privacy and summary statistics techniques
to support private analysis of large aggregation-based datasets, such as those
generated by location-based services. Current implementations in this domain
overlook the inherent structure of spatial data, failing to account for the
interdependencies present in such data, which is critical for conducting
statistical evaluations. To address this gap, we integrate a Gaussian Graphical
Model to capture the dependencies present in the data, while using the
Mallows' Distance to measure distance between distributions. Our framework not
only ensures the privacy of individual data contributors by employing a
combination of differential privacy and zero-constrained mechanisms, but it
also safeguards against data losses resulting from privacy decisions taken by
contributors. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we establish a metric
that quantifies the impact of data privacy on analysis accuracy, which enables
data collectors to determine the optimal level of privacy based on predetermined
evaluation standards. Our methodology is comprehensive, allowing collectors to
set, implement and validate privacy boundaries in accordance with their needs. 
Finally, we demonstrate the applicability and effectiveness of our approach via
real-world case studies in the location-based services domain. To facilitate
reproducibility, full details of our methodology, data collections and analysis
processes are accessible via an open-source repository hosted on GitHub.

Processional encoding methods have significantly improved the performance of various tasks, especially when dealing with code-mixed text. Recent research suggests that autoencoding positional information can be an effective way to utilize positional encoding. Building on this insight, we propose the application of autoencoding positional encoding to language models. However, current methods that autoencode positional information do not account for the sentential level. Therefore, we aim to overcome this limitation by introducing Sentential-Autoencoded Positional Encoding (SAPE). Furthermore, we recognize the potential for improved modeling if sentential-level positional encoding can be combined with word-level positional encoding. Therefore, we develop Word-Level Autoencoded Positional Encoding (WAP) by integrating both levels. We apply SAPE and WAP to the Indic-code-mixed language classification task, achieving remarkable results, with WAP outperforming baseline models by 4% in terms of accuracy. Notably, the combination of WAP and transformer-based models results in an 5% improvement in accuracy compared to the baseline models. Components of WAP were also independently tested, with Subword-Autoencoded Positional Encoding (SAP) emerging as the top-performing method, achieving 5% better performance than the baseline models. Furthermore, we observe significant improvements in model robustness, especially when dealing with noisy code-mixing data. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the efficacy of autoencoding positional encoding at the sentential, word, and subword levels. Due to the open-source nature of our work, we hope it to be a valuable resource for the natural language processing community. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/anchorclt/SAPE-WAPE. As for the data, it is available at https://huggingface.com datasets/SAPE-WAPE. H$_{3}$S is considered a prime material for room-temperature superconductors due to its exceptional efficiency of converting pressure to superconducting properties. Through theoretical analysis using a simple model, it has been determined that the enhancement of superconductivity from pressure and chemical potential contributions follows the equation $\gamma = \gamma_p + \gamma_m = \frac{9}{2\hbar v_F^2} \frac{\partial \mu_S}{\partial p} + \frac{9}{2\hbar v_F^2} \frac{\partial \mu_S}{\partial n_s}$, where the first term represents how pressure influences superconductivity and the second term represents superconductivity's response to changes in sulfur concentration. By using density functional theory to determine key parameters, it has been found that the isotope effect coefficient $\beta$ in H$_{3}$S at ambient pressure is dominated by pressure variations, accounting for approximately 60% of the coefficient and predicting a significant drop as pressure approaches the superconducting transition. Conversely, the contribution of chemical potential variations is relatively stable and predictably increases with pressure in H$_{3}$S superconductors. By taking into account recent experiments indicating a superconducting critical pressure of around 200 GPa, it has been determined that the isotope effect coefficient $\beta$ in H$_{3}$S could potentially reach values suitable for high-temperature superconductors under such extreme pressures. Nonetheless, the analysis suggests that lower-order electron-like excitations may significantly contribute to the superconducting response in H$_{3}$S beyond simple electron-phonon interactions. By further leveraging theoretical calculations of H$_{3}$S structural and dynamical properties, it has been determined that lower energy excitations could potentially be transferred to higher energy excitations through structural and dynamical adjustments as pressure increases. Consequently, it has been hypothesized that lower energy excitations could potentially be transferred to higher energy excitations and that further research may reveal a more complex interaction scheme involving multiple energy components in H$_{3}$S superconductors. As such, H$_{3}$S may be uniquely positioned between conventional and unconventional superconductors due to its distinct phonon-driven interactions. Finally, the research suggests that the innovative use of phonon-driven interactions in H$_{3}$S superconductors could potentially be used to develop multi-energy component superconductors by leveraging corresponding electron-like excitations and phonon-like excitations at distinct energy points.

This contrasts with the behavior of hyperelliptic curves, which do exhibit non-zero classes. Next, we've established that weighted projective surfaces of higher degree also never display a non-zero first Mumford-Morita-Miller class. Interestingly, this implies that a general projective surface will only exhibit a non-zero first MMM class when it's a super-rigid member of its weight class, such as a compact Riemann surface or a hyperelliptic curve. We've further observed that non-trivial automorphisms prevent the presence of a non-zero first MMM class on a general projective surface. We've derived a formula for the second Mumford-Morita-Miller class of a Riemann surface, which reveals that it's always zero for surfaces with non-trivial automorphisms. Using this, we've shown that the second MMM class of any Riemann surface can be represented as a linear combination of its Albanese class and the classes of its 1-1 coverings. Consequently, we've deduced that the first MMM class generated from the square root of the canonical line bundle on a Riemann surface or a weighted projective surface is indeed a first-order invariant. Crowdsourcing is becoming increasingly popular, with crowdfunding specifically seeing significant growth. Research has primarily focused on understanding crowd behavior through statistical analysis of project information. Meanwhile, research on crowd dynamics is rare. This paper introduces a method to model crowd behavior based on user actions throughout the funding period. By examining user behavior over time, we can distinguish between different types of crowd responses and pinpoint switches in behavior patterns. In contrast to fixed feature vectors, time-dependent representations of crowd behavior allow us to identify shifts in behavior caused by external factors, such as the creator's response to feedback from funders. When comparing crowd features to project and funder characteristics, our results show that crowd behavior makes significant predictive contributions. Ultimately, capturing the dynamic nature of crowd behavior adds value to the understanding of crowdfunding. The code for replicating our analysis can be found at https://github.com/appletselyakov/crowd_dynamics.git. Research questions centered on (a) identifying changes in crowd behavior, (b) discerning natural and induced behaviors, and (c) evaluating the predictive value of crowd behavior. All data were accessed through Kickstarter's API, which provided information for 883 projects with 51,485 user actions from a random sample of projects with user activity. The analysis revealed that crowd behavior can be modeled using a Markov process consisting of four distinct states: positive, negative, mixed, and inactive. Transition probabilities were estimated empirically. To differentiate between natural and induced crowd behaviors, we examined fundamental series of actions. Predicting project success became significantly more accurate when incorporating crowd behavior, with the area under the ROC curve rising from 0.71 to 0.76. The study found that crowd behavior can effectively supplement project information in forecasting fundraising outcomes. As a key contribution, our research shows that crowd behavior can be effectively modeled using time-dependent representations, identified through the application of the k-means algorithm, and can be distinguished from project and funder characteristics. Moreover, capturing the dynamic nature of crowd behavior adds predictive value to the understanding of crowdfunding. The study found that crowd behavior can effectively predict fundraising outcomes, and it is viable to distinguish between natural and induced crowd behaviors. Key limitations of the research involve the constraints of data accessibility and the complexity of modeling human behavior. The research primarily focused on understanding the nature of crowd behavior and its predictive value, and it explored the application of crowd behavior to funding periods but did not delve into the reasoning behind funders' actions. Semi-supervised node classification in graph neural networks is a crucial issue, and pseudo-labeling has been proposed to address it by enlarging the training set with labeled nodes. Nevertheless, conventional pseudo-labeling techniques may assign labels to nodes already labeled, leading to label contamination, which negatively impacts the graph neural network's performance. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel pseudo-labeling technique that prevents label contamination and uses graph structure to select reliable pseudo-labels. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms existing pseudo-labeling techniques and rival deep self-supervised node classification methods on diverse graph datasets. The code for this work is available on GitHub at the address https://github.com/ShuoXu-TIT/GraphPseudoLabeling.
