The traditional approach in out-of-distribution (OoD) detection considers any data point outside a trained model's prediction confidence interval as anomalous. However, this strategy often leads to false positives when encountering challenging data, whether it be from shifted in-distribution data or truly OoD instances. To improve this tactic, researchers have attempted to define a clearer distinction between in-distribution and out-of-distribution data, utilizing additional labeled data or training datasets as guides. Despite these efforts, most current methods are unable to accurately detect shifts in training data or reserve reliance on reliance on heuristic boundaries around the normal data point distribution. In response to these limitations, this paper presents a new strategy called Relative Confidence Threshold (RCT), which establishes a more robust OoD detection framework. RCT relies solely on the posterior distributions generated during model training, allowing it to effectively distinguish internal anomalies within the normal data point distribution. In addition, RCT rakes advantage of the power of Bayesian inference, integrating data point uncertainty into the detection process. As a result, RCT outperforms state-of-the-art methods in challenging scenarios,, including synthetic data, image data, and multi-class classification tasks. Importantly, RCT does not rely on additional labeled data, making it a more practical solution for real-world applications. We explore the potential for a specific class of regular resynchronizers to transform non-deterministic two-way word transducers into equivalent one-way transducers, focusing on those with a bounded and regular pattern. This involves the use of origin-marked one-way transducers, which have a designated start symbol marked as '∗'. This marked symbol is a pre-defined exception, crucial for addressing the question. For regular sets R, S, the origin-marked one-way transducer problem asks if there's a regular set S' such that S' multiplied by ∗ equals R multiplied by ∃S'. This is an extension of the celebrated Schützenberger theorem. We find that regular sets S and R determine whether a non-deterministic two-way word transducer can be transformed into an origin-equivalent one-way transducer. This means such a resynchronizer exists for S and R if S contains the intersection of R multiplied by ∃S'1 and R multiplied by ∃S'2, where ∃S'1 and ∃S'2 are the positive and null closed subsets of S'. This shows that the origin-marked one-way transducer problem is solvable for specific instances, but not generally. This contrasts with the two-way case, where such a resynchronizer exists and is not necessarily bounded. We find that boundedness doesn't apply universally, but proves crucial for ensuring that the resynchronizer works with origin-marked one-way transducers. This leads to the conclusion that the origin-marked one-way transducer problem is in the class NP. We have conducted a thorough study of the atmosphere of GJ 229B, a benchmark object for understanding brown dwarfs and giant planets. Our analysis combines data from the SPIRIT and IRAC instruments on board Spitzer, and reveals that the best-fitting atmospheric model features a strong methane signal, characteristic of warm, subsolar temperatures. This discovery indicates that the atmosphere dominates the system, and that dust cannot be present as suggested by previous studies. Our findings and analytical methods are comparable to those used for the atmosphere of 2MASS 1207-3845, another system consisting of a brown dwarf and a giant planet. By modeling the relative brightness of these two objects, we have determined a distance of approximately 7.8 parsecs between GJ 229B and its host star. This estimate is crucial for further studying the dynamical history of this system, and potentially discovering similar objects. Our research also opens doors for exploring the formation processes of intermediate objects with properties falling between those of planets and stars. Lastly, our work highlights the utility of combining data from space-based and ground-based observatories for understanding the properties of celestial bodies.

A future generation of high-energy particle colliders, specifically the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), is poised to test the Standard Model further. One critical test involves the investigation of CP violation in top quark production and decay. High-precision measurements of this CP-violating phase, known as $\Delta\phi_{t\bar{t}}$, are expected, with a goal of achieving an uncertainty of $0.02\pi$ or better. This phase, which arises from the interplay of top quark pair production and decay, is crucial in testing enhancements of its measurement inherent to new physics models. To optimize this test, we suggest enhancing the accuracy of $\Delta\phi_{t\bar{t}}$ by incorporating an asymmetry parameter, $A_{t\bar{t}}$, which amplifies the sensitivity to new physics when coupled with additional variables. Specifically, a novel input, referred to as the Sivers asymmetry, linked to spin and transverse momentum, has the potential to significantly boost the precision of $\Delta\phi_{t\bar{t}}$ with a precision of $0.02\phi$ without requiring additional data and can serve as a powerful tool to both test the Standard Model and detect new physics in top quark-based observations at the LHC. As a result, the research, will offer far reaching contributions in the area of new physics research at the LHC. Moreover, the study, will provide the initial investigation of the Sivers asymmetry in top quark production and decay, a topic yet to be explored by theory and experiment. With the anticipated precision of $\Delta\phi_{t\bar{t}}$, this work, can offer critical insights into the internal dynamics of hadronic collisions, by providing the first measurement of the Sivers asymmetry. In addition, the research, can offer valuable information regarding the transverse momentum distribution, by making use of an experimentally verified, normalized differential cross-section, $d\sigma/dp_T$, which can be compared to state-of-the-art theoretical predictions. Ultimately, the proposed analysis, appears to be a promising strategy, not just for new physics detection at the LHC, but for a wide range of related research topics in particle physics. In this vein, the research, presents an exhaustive analysis of the theoretical aspects of the Sivers asymmetry and the momentum distribution in top quark production and decay. We create computational models to estimate aerosolized particle counts around an infected person, considering both simple and complex scenarios. A basic "well-mixed" model treats the space as a single homogeneous zone where particles are evenly distributed, unlike more sophisticated approaches such as the "coupled multiplier method" that account for complex air flow and particle behavior. By simulating particle movement and settling, our models calculate the concentration of particles within a specified area, such as a room or vehicle, under different operating conditions including various fan settings. Our study focuses on cashless payment systems in China, specifically the wearable devices used at McDonald's restaurants in Shanghai, by investigating the impact of different particle sizes and infection rates. Both models are capable of predicting similar results when infection rates are low but diverge significantly when infection rates are high, placing the least restrictive limits on particle size when using the well-mixed model. Our work has important implications for understanding the spread of COVID-19 and designing airborne infection control measures. Researchers have successfully measured the half-lives of two rare isotopes, $^{137}$Te and $^{135}$Te, which undergo beta decay. To understand these transitions, they used a detailed nuclear structure model and compared it with measurements of the decay's strength. This comparison revealed that a particular level within the nucleus, known as a quasiparticle phonon coupled (QPC) state, dominates these beta-transitions. What's more, in $^{137}$Te, this QPC state is formed through the combination of a neutron-proton excitation and a single particle situated outside of a closed nuclear shell, whereas in $^{135}$Te, the relevant state is formed by a neutron-proton excitation with two particles situated outside of a closed shell. Additionally, in $^{135}$Te, a significant portion of the decay strength is absorbed by another nuclear state, known as a particle-hole state. This new information provides valuable insights into the intricate structure of nuclei. Based on the gathered data, researchers have proposed limits on a particular type of nuclear transition, known as a long-range weak interaction, which could potentially explain a particular type of nuclear decay observed in other studies. This new study provides the tightest limits on these interactions yet proposed. Finally, in $^{137}$Te, researchers have discovered that a particular type of nuclear transition, known as a beta-transformation followed by the emission of a gamma ray, is significantly more likely to occur when the initial nuclear state is formed by a neutron-proton excitation, rather than by a single particle situated outside of a closed shell. This new information provides valuable insights into the relationships between nuclear structures and their corresponding decay patterns. We have developed a set of automatic exchange rate calculation methods that can be applied to diverse monetary systems. These methods are underpinned by two novel mathematical theorems that can identify unauthorized exchange practices. Our approach to calculating exchange rates is grounded in a unique geometric interpretation, allowing us to draw precise boundaries around the range of possible exchange rates. By using these methods, which are consistent with established monetary theory, we can effectively detect irregular exchange activities. We have successfully tested our exchange rate calculation methods using data from the official websites of central banks in the United States and Europe, as well as by creating a web scraper to gather data on exchange rates from various foreign banks. Notably, our automated analysis uncovered multiple instances of potential exchange program violations that have significant implications for money laundering and tax evasion. By using our unique theorem, we can formally verify that the official exchange rates published by central banks align with the theoretically determined exchange rates, thereby confirming their validity. Our innovative exchange rate calculation methods provide valuable insights into the structure of monetary systems and can be used to develop AI-powered tools to detect suspicious activity in exchange programs. We introduce a novel kernel-based method that adapts dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) to operate in complex data spaces transformed by nonlinear kernel functions. Each data point is represented by a set of grid points, and dynamics between these points are modeled through the application of a linear operator. This approach translates to a linear eigenproblem that can capture complex behaviors. However, such linear representations are insufficient when dealing with data spaces or systems that have nonlinear properties. To address this limitation, we develop a method that uses kernel functions to linearize the relationship between data points and their successors in time. This novel kernel-based DMD (KDMD) method leads to more accurate predictions of system behavior compared to traditional DMD methods. To facilitate the application of KDMD to large-scale systems, we propose a method that approximates the kernel function using random linear projections, significantly reducing computational costs without compromising accuracy. This approach allows us to train a robust low-dimensional representation of complex systems with numerous degrees of freedom, and predict their behavior with great accuracy. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, we test it on data from experimental campaigns involving the vibration of a plate and a panel. These experiments reveal the stunning predictive power of our kernel-based DMD method. To the best of our knowledge, this work marks the first application of dynamic mode decomposition to nonlinear systems of the highest dimensionality. The game of chess has been a benchmark for artificial intelligence since the iconic computer program Eliza, and advancements in algorithms and available data have made it possible to effectively apply machine learning to the game. A pre-existing dataset of 2 million chess openings was used to assess the application of the Economic Fitness and Complexity algorithm. This method evaluates the strategic and tactical competitiveness of openings by simulating player behavior based on their skills and the strengths of the openings. The results revealed a 12-point difference in efficiency between the top and bottom of the International Chess Federation's (FIDE) rating system. In essence, the approach demonstrated that certain aspects of chess play can be viewed as an evolutionary process influenced by the fitness of player and opening combinations. This unique algorithm has the potential to improve player training by recommending more suitable openings to players based on their skills and preferences. Additionally, it may be adapted to assess the competitiveness of other cultural, scientific, or linguistic constructs known as memes. The study's success relies on its ability to accurately predict the FIDE ratings by analyzing data from 2020, and applying this understanding to analyze the impact of the COVID pandemic on chess players' skills and the strategic and tactical advantages of their chosen openings. The findings show that top players maintained their advantages, while lower-rated players experienced a decline of up to 50 tokens in fitness and 10 points in rating. This unexpected response to the pandemic is found to be significantly correlated with the global economic disruption at the time. The research reveals that top players in the 2000-2020 period exhibited increased competitiveness in their openings over time, and that this trend is linked to the release of pre-trained neural networks. The study's findings are validated by accurately forecasting the 2020 FIDE ratings, and applying the Economic Fitness and Complexity algorithm to identify the most promising chess openings for players of all skill levels. As a result, the recommended opening library can be used to enhance player training, and the analysis of the toggle probability can aid in identifying the cultural, scientific, or linguistic constructs known as memes that are most responsive to changes in the chess world. The potential applications of this research include assessing the impact of learning strategies on the development of player skills, evaluating the effectiveness of different training approaches, and exploring the link between cultural, scientific, or linguistic constructs known as memes that are present in the chess universe. The study's findings are grounded in an extensive literature review of the role of artificial intelligence in chess, and the research is made more accessible through the use of an accompanying video and code repositories

This process is pivotal in understanding the potential supernovae resulting from such systems, as well as the possibility of forming strange stars or black holes through this process. In recent research, the authors have developed a detailed binary evolution code, utilizing a Python-based program, and applied it to various models of AIC. Their studies involved models of stable and unstable mass accumulation, including scenarios involving external mass feeding, and examined the predictive power of their code in predicting supernovae and compact remnant formation. This code is designed to facilitate further studies of AIC and can be accessed through a public repository, where users can view executed runs and obtain guidance on its usage. In addition to its application in the BE of stable systems, the code is also adaptable for use in supercritical collapse, as well as for users who wish to implement relativistic core collapse, utilizing a obtained SEDM to simulate this process. In the near future, the code will be updated to incorporate improvements in the input of core properties, as well as to enhance its ability to utilize relativistic ESDMs. This update will significantly expand its scope in the study of AIC, particularly in the formation of strange stars and black holes. Reconstructing complex 3D objects accurately from partial information can be a challenging task. In contrast to 2D image-based object recognition, which focuses on detailed representations, our problem involves retrieving a complex 3D shape from a sketch that captures its overall features. Past studies on 3D sketch recognition employed geometric and image-based methods. Unlike these approaches, we found that geometric methods outperform image-based ones due to the abstract nature of 3D sketches. To build upon this success, we propose a new framework that selectively uses additional shape information to refine geometric retrievals. Our experimental results show that this framework surpasses existing geometric methods by a significant margin when evaluated on the ShapeNet dataset. Moreover, we demonstrate that incorporating more abstract global features can improve geometric retrieval performance, and we provide theoretical evidence for this finding. To facilitate future research, we have made our code and dataset analysis available for download. Our study's success indicates that combining multi-modal information can lead to state-of-the-art performance in 3D sketch recognition. Moreover, we show that geometric methods have the potential to surpass traditional image-based approaches even in the partial view setting. Lastly, we provide a new interpretation of the partial view problem as a 3D sketch recognition task and show potential future directions for research. Our code and dataset analyses are available for download at https://github.com/amanbasu/selectively_geometric.

The exoplanet HD80606b undergoes a substantial heat transition as it passes close to its host star every 111 days. Researchers captured critical thermal images of the planet during its closest approach, utilizing the NICMOS camera on the Hubble Space Telescope. They were able to gather high-resolution thermal maps in three wavelength ranges: 0.8, 0.6, and 1.5 microns. These images showed that HD806b's temperature dropped to about 1270 K (similar to the temperature of tellurian models) when it was 0.04 AU from the star, despite expectations of a higher temperature. They observed a strong temperature variations of 750 K in the map taken at a distance of 0.06 AU from the star, with higher temperatures on the forward-side and lower on the backside. This sided temperature difference is most prominent in the 0.6 micron wavelength range and less pronounced in the other two. They also detected signs of a cold spot near the star and attributed it to atmospheric frost on the surface. Models based on a simple radiative model accurately reproduced the observed time-series data at all three wavelengths. This was extended to canonical ensembles in a previous study, where the minimum possible energy for the black hole was established, taking into account its charge and temperature. Here, we apply the same methodology to the black hole's magnetic properties, which leads to the prediction that in canonical ensembles, the magnetic charge will decrease and the mass will remain constant. Conversely, when the magnetic properties are ignored, the mass will decrease as required by the weak gravity conjecture. Additionally, our findings align with the theoretical limitation on the mass-to-charge ratio imposed by the membrane paradigm. Furthermore, we examine the thermodynamic stability of the canonical ensemble and the weak gravity conjecture, and our analysis suggests that these conditions are not simultaneously satisfied. Finally, we investigate the thermodynamic stability of the canonical ensemble when the black hole undergoes an electric-to-magnetic transition, which occurs when its magnetic properties begin to dominate. We detail the requirements for this phase transition and the inherent instability of the canonical ensemble, which arises due to the difference in behavior of the mass and charge as temperature varies. This instability persists even after the phase transition, where the mass still does not meet the stability criterion, until it reaches its critical value. Conversely, when the magnetic properties are ignored, the mass does not reach its critical value, but rather diverges as the temperature approaches its critical value. Lastly, all of our findings are applicable to non-extremal black holes. Conversely, the extremal black hole meets the weak gravity conjecture, but only if its mass and charge are proportional to each other, as would be expected for an extremal black hole. This study combines two established techniques in reinforcement learning to accelerate training efficiency. First, introducing intrinsic goals alongside extrinsic rewards leverages learned representations to dynamically set objectives based on a model's internal state, promoting more efficient exploration. Experiments across diverse environments demonstrate a notable increase in training efficiency when incorporating intrinsic goals. When extrinsic rewards are reintroduced, the intrinsic objectives evaporate, and the agent refocuses on the tuned tasks. We find that wrapping a policy in an intrinsic-extrinsic learner enhances performance and accelerates learning. For example, in Atari games, this hybrid approach yields state-of-the-art results, outperforming previous methods that utilized intrinsic goals in Montezuma's Revenge and achieving comparable success in Pitfall. Additionally, this technique proves effective in multi-goal tasks, as shown by its application to the Keyworld environment. Overall, the proposed method effectively bridges the gaps between intrinsic and extrinsic reward learning and multi-goal reinforcement learning. We explore new investigations into the parameterized complexity class FPT and the relationship between directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) and constraints represented as Boolean formulas with limited variables and gate operations. Specifically, we demonstrate that various properties involving low treewidth subgraphs within a DAG can be solved efficiently when considering a limited number of variables and gate operations in relation to the treewidth parameter. Moreover, we establish a new upper bound for efficiently solving the subgraph isomorphism problem on a DAG by treating it as a binary classification task constrained by a Boolean formula and treewidth parameter. Interestingly, this problem cannot be solved efficiently when the treewidth parameter is set free, even under the assumption of a limited number of variables and gate operations. Lastly, we investigate the parameterized complexity of finding a minimal treewidth-k subgraph within a DAG, showing it to be efficiently solvable when the number of sources is limited, but inherently intractable when the treewidth parameter is set free or the number of sources is allowed to exceed linear constraint size. These findings contribute meaningfully to the study of parameterized algorithmics on DAGs. Furthermore, we introduce a new class of reductive positive results involving low treewidth subgraphs within a DAG, encompassing properties like node and edge connectivity, isolated node detection, and cycle presence. This article defends the utilization of complex numbers in Quantum Mechanics, arguing that they are inherent components of the theory. We illustrate the significance of complex coefficients in Schrodinger's equation by deriving it from a classical action integral, utilizing the principle of least action. We also examine the mathematical properties of Hilbert spaces, justifying the necessity of using complex coefficients in quantum states. We find that the dual role of the Bra-Ket notation in representing inner products and expectation values is well-reasoned in light of this formulation. We conclude by discussing the common issues with real-vector-space formulations of Quantum Mechanics. We suggest that the true novelty of Quantum Mechanics lies in the predictable association of uncertainty rather than the uncertainty itself, an aspect that real-vector-space formulations fail to capture. We propose the term 'complex-plausible' to describe theories that incorporate complex numbers, such as Quantum Mechanics, in contrast to'real-compatible' theories, like Classical Mechanics. We then explore the term 'complex-plausible' as a paradigm for other quantum generalizations of Classical Mechanics, including reformulated theories and alternative interpretations of wave function and operator roles. We examine the scope of 'complex-plausible' explanations, whether confined to specific measurement outcomes or extending more broadly. We then apply the term 'complex-plausible' to probabilistic and deterministic formulations of quantum mechanics, leading to the notion of 'complex-plausible' being a more fundamental aspect of nature than mere uncertainty. We then explore the possibility of reducing 'complex-plausible' to'real-compatible' structures through future developments, an aspect that would not necessarily occur. We then explore the possibility of multi-threaded 'complex-plausible' and'real-compatible' interpretations of physical laws, an aspect that would result in quantum mechanics and classical mechanics being formulated on different thread assumptions. We then examine the possibility of common origins for real-vector-space formulations and complex numbers in quantum mechanics. The steady-state flow equation for groundwater can be represented by Darcy's law, which becomes straightforward when the hydraulic conductivity is dependent on vertical position. By integrating Darcy's equation from the ground surface to a depth 'b', we derive a formula that simplifies the flow equation. This simplified equation is useful for situations involving uniform groundwater flow and a linear change in hydraulic conductivity with depth. Our approach draws upon the concept of flow-weighted average, which revolves around the idea of averaging properties across horizontal cross-sections. We then generalize this approach to vertical anisotropy by considering the flow equation for nonlinear hydraulic conductivity. Our generalization yields a useful relationship and a consistent interpretation of flow-weighted averages. These results are crucial for estimating average flow and solving problems related to regional flow. Our methodology also lends itself to applications beyond groundwater hydrology and can be extended to other problems involving integrable systems. Moreover, our analysis is not limited to one-dimensional scenarios and can be expanded to multi-dimensional settings where the flow rates are known. This study investigates the ability of an O3-UV reactor to remove sulfur dioxide under various conditions, with a focus on two key factors: reactor size and treatment time. The research reveals that as reactor size decreases or treatment time shortens, its removal efficiency also declines. Furthermore, the data shows that the reactor's capacity to remove sulfur dioxide grows in proportion to the square of the reactor size, but this finding contrasts with the treatment time regime, for which a linear relationship holds. In addition, the study identifies that the reactor's removal efficiency for sulfur dioxide is directly influenced by the ratio of ozone to sulfur dioxide concentrations, as well as the UV radiation dose applied. As a result, we develop a unified model that can accurately model the sulfur dioxide removal process across a broad range of conditions. The newly developed model exhibits excellent agreement with the experimental data obtained from various operating conditions, providing a useful tool for predicting the sulfur dioxide removal process in the O3-UV reactor. In particular, the model can be utilized to estimate the required ozone and UV radiation doses necessary to achieve a desired removal efficiency for sulfur dioxide in air. Based on this model, we investigate the impact of different factors, including reactor size, treatment time, and gas flow rate, on the removal of sulfur dioxide, with our results showing that a small-scale reactor has a lower capacity to remove sulfur dioxide compared to a larger one, an effect that becomes more pronounced at shorter treatment times. Additionally, the study reveals that as the gas flow rate increases, the removal efficiency of sulfur dioxide declines. As a result, using a model developed from first-principle-based kinetics, we demonstrate the potential of the O3-UV technology to remove sulfur dioxide from air by achieving a removal efficiency of nearly 90% under certain conditions, with a large reactor exhibiting significantly higher removal efficiencies compared to a small reactor. Specifically, while a small-scale reactor can only achieve a removal efficiency lower than 50%, a large reactor can attain removal efficiencies above 80% when operated at higher gas flow rates. Therefore, the O3-UV technology has considerable potential to remove sulfur dioxide from air effectively. In conclusion, the study provides valuable insights into the removal of sulfur dioxide using the O3-UV technology, offering important implications for utilizing this promising technology to mitigate air pollution effectively. As neuromorphic accelerators shift from hardware evaluation to software development, a vital need arises for suitable simulation environments. Based on System-On-Chip (SoC) architecture, these simulators are developed using Model-Based Design in MATLAB, with neuromorphic accelerators defined as Intellectual Property (IP) blocks. We focus on three distinct virtual platform configurations: software-based, hardware-assisted, and automatic hardware-assisted simulations. Our analysis covers three aspects: the accuracy of neuromorphic accelerator modeling, the accuracy of external component modeling, and the overall simulation speed. We reveal that hardware-assisted simulation boasts the fastest speed, though it requires manual compilation, whereas automatic hardware-assisted simulation showcases promising potential, despite requiring extended compilation time. Nonetheless, both hardware-assisted options prove to be more accurate than the software-based option. Importantly, our findings highlight the necessity for more precise modeling of memory modules in virtual platforms. These conclusions pave the way for further investigation into other virtual platform configurations, ultimately aiming to identify the most suitable simulation architecture for neuromorphic accelerators, as identified through a thorough evaluation of trade-offs between accuracy, complexity, and speed. The ultimate goal is to define the most optimal simulation architecture for neuromorphic accelerators, as evaluated by considering these trade-offs. Moreover, our work suggests that hardware-assisted simulation may serve as a potential solution for simulating neuromorphic accelerators in scenarios where ultra-fast simulation speeds are crucial. In contrast, automatic hardware-assisted simulation could be an effective approach when high accuracy is a primary concern. Lastly, software-based simulation may be suitable for educational purposes, given its relatively fast speed, though it lacks the necessary precision for actual hardware testing. As a result, it could potentially be used as a preliminary step before transitioning to more accurate hardware-assisted simulations. Here, we provide guidance on when to utilize each of these simulation strategies, thus facilitating the selection of the most suitable option for neuromorphic accelerator modeling and simulation. Moreover, our work highlights several memory-related issues that require attention in virtual platform configurations, with potential implications for other hardware components as well. We introduce Indecision Trees, a novel model that addresses the limitations of current methods by learning from partially labeled data. Unlike conventional models, which require complete labeling, Indecision Trees can make informed predictions based on incomplete or ambiguous labels. This ability extends to learning from datasets with conflicting annotations, mislabeled data, or unknown labels. The algorithm represents each sample as a path within a decision tree, aiming to group samples with similar attributes. A prediction is then a consensus reached among multiple models, each describing a subset of the dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that Indecision Trees achieve high accuracy when trained on partially labeled data and exhibit robustness in the presence of labeling errors. Notably, their predictive power approaches that of traditional decision trees while benefiting from the incorporation of additional information. Indecision Trees may find applications in high-noise labeling scenarios, such as working with datasets annotated by AI or crowdsourced, or in cases where labeling is a costly or time-consuming process. Our objective is to enhance the performance of approximate algorithms used for this search by incorporating early abandoning to prevent unnecessary calculations. This approach can be integrated with existing pruning methods without modifying their strategy or efficiency. We demonstrate the effectiveness of early abandoning through experimental results showing significant speed gains of up to 3.5 times for concrete datasets, with a average increase of approximately 2 times, as well as a high level of accuracy with an Labeled Distance Matrix score of 0.95 for our best configuration. The optimal result was achieved using Lifting Index with a Threshold-Based method and an Adaboost classifier. This methodology has the benefit of adaptability, allowing it to work with diverse pruning methods, datasets, and classification models, making it suitable for various scenarios. Moreover, the source code is accessible on GitHub under the repository name TSSAEB.

These observations suggest that the choice of methods is crucial for achieving efficiency with early abandoning.

This study presents a model for project-based assessment that utilizes feedback from code reviews to inform both programming and feedback grades. The code review feedback is treated as a prior learning objective, and students are allowed to learn from it, but only to the extent reflected in their subsequent code changes. The model's effectiveness is tested on a dataset comprising 109 projects from an introductory programming course, where projects with minimal code modifications are compared to those modified extensively. The results show that incorporating code review feedback into the grading model improves accuracy and reduces bias, particularly for groups traditionally underrepresented in the field, and also uncovers a hidden bias among instructors. The model's ability to utilize code review feedback has a small but significant positive impact on grades, and its aggregation mechanism does not disadvantage students who submit code with minimal modifications. Such a mechanism may be seen as unfavorable, but the evidence suggests it has a small positive effect on learning objectives measured through code changes. The model's potential limitations, along with areas for further research, are also highlighted. The model, code, and data are publicly available. https://doi.org/10.1145/3531114.3531115, and https://github.com/krishanrusso/adaptive-curriculum-grades. Interpretable AI is crucial to comprehending why black-box models have made particular decisions. Simplifying complex models into more understandable formats can shed light on their workings. In this study, we explore the potential of symbolic model surrogates in shedding light on the decision-making processes of black-box classifiers. By using an automatic learning method to create symbolic models from data, we can gain a deeper understanding of how these black-box models arrive at their conclusions. In our research, we analyzed the admission decisions made by the Harvard University admissions board in the 1970s, as described in the "Course of His Grace" dataset, using both a black-box classifier and a symbolic model to illustrate the decision-making processes and to highlight the potential for bias in the black-box model. Our research suggests that symbolic model surrogates can facilitate in-depth analysis of black-box models and aid in identifying any biases within them. In addition, they may also reduce the need for additional, computationally expensive data sets when auditing deep learning models. In accordance with the principles of transparent AI, our research aims to promote the use of both symbolic model surrogates and more interpretable machine learning methods. Over-smoothing significantly hampers the performance of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs). While this limitation has been extensively studied, the underlying causes and their implications in algorithm design are not yet fully comprehended. This research provides a mathematical proof of the over-smoothing phenomenon in GCNs and identifies the underlying factors contributing to it. Furthermore, it proposes an efficient approach to mitigate over-smoothing by reducing the number of convolutional layers in GCNs. However, this method comes with a cost of decreased expressiveness. To balance both concerns, it is essential to design a network with the optimal number of convolutional layers. To address this challenge, a novel lower bound for the eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix in GCNs is formulated, and the condition number of the normalized adjacency matrix is also analyzed. Based on these findings, a simple yet effective method for determining the optimal number of convolutional layers in GCNs is developed. The proposed approach is general and can be applied to various graph neural networks. The research is accompanied by empirical evidence validating the theoretical analysis and the designed algorithm. Simplified models representing a single type of mediator in dark matter particle production were previously studied. In this work, we consider the cases with multiple types of mediators, including a pair of identical scalar mediators and a pair of vector mediators. The boundary of the dark matter particle production cross-section limits is determined for these simplified models, incorporating constraints from monopole dark matter, lepton number, and 3L decay searches as well as LHC searches for resonance production. The derived constraints are compared with those from a pair of vector mediators in a more complex, 'y-y-y' type interaction where the three vector mediators have different masses. The results show that the production cross-section limits for the two types of double mediator scenarios are similar to those found in previous studies on single mediator models, often surpassing the 'y-y-y' type interaction scenario only at very high mass ranges. The study also shows that while the triple production of mediator particles may occur at a much lower rate than the production of a pair plus an extra particle in these scenarios, it could become the dominant process when the mass of one of the participating particles approaches its maximum possible value. The derivation of dark matter particle production limits, specifically focusing on a dark matter-proton interaction, under a scenario where dark matter is produced through a pair of vector mediators with similar masses is another aspect of this study. We introduce QFRs as an alternative set of variables describing e+e- annihilation into hadrons. These new functions focus on the transverse motion of partons within hadrons and are directly related to QFDs. By combining QFRs and QFDs, one can gain a deeper understanding of hadron formation. The QFRs and QFDs are complementary views of the same processes. The joint representation is more informative than either alone. The joint analysis of these quantities can provide the most accurate extraction of the parton momentum distribution within hadrons. The joint measurement also offers the most precise determination of the strong coupling constant, αs. The relationship between QFDs and QFRs is compared to the connection between jet profiles and fragmentation functions. While fragmentation functions describe the longitudinal motion of hadrons, QFDs reveal detailed aspects of this motion. Similarly, QFRs reveal the transverse motion of partons, which is a key aspect not revealed by fragmentation functions. The QFRs are further compared to saturation models, which suggest that transverse momentum distributions are largely determined at an early stage of the parton formation process. We also discuss the prospects for measuring QFRs using recent data from e+e- annihilation experiments, such as those conducted at Belle, Belle II, and CDF. The measurement of QFRs may be challenging because the parton transverse momentum is highly correlated with the jet momentum. The successful measurement of QFRs may require the collaboration of physicists and engineers who specialize in both particle physics and quantum chromodynamics. The potential for measuring QFRs presents an exciting new opportunity for contributing to our understanding of the structure of partons within hadrons. The possibility of measuring QFRs also offers promising prospects for advancing research in many areas, such as tiny primordial primordially generated leptoquark dark matter, semitauons, R-parity violating supersymmetry, and quantum gravity, to name just a few. Researchers are particularly interested in creating epitaxial materials on graphene due to its unique properties. A recent study successfully grown BaTiO$_3$ on graphene using a molecular beam epitaxy method with varying growth temperatures. The results showed that different temperature ranges produce unique substrate-layers combinations, such as a BaTiO$_3$ layer on hexagonal graphene at temperatures below 300 K. The properties of these combinations were investigated using four probe spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, and electron diffraction. The findings show that the layers have a 30 degree rotational mismatch with the hexagonal graphene, but not with square graphene layers. The property of being epitaxial is sensitive to both the substrate type and growth temperature. The team also observed that the layers on square graphene have a different structural property compared to their counterparts grown on hexagonal graphene. The properties of these combinations can be tailored by adjusting the graphene preparation methods. A particular preparation method was found to eliminate the rotational mismatch with the hexagonal graphene, resulting in a 0 degree epitaxial alignment. The ability to control the properties of these combinations could lead to the development of unique electronic and multifunctional devices. The research shows that combining graphene with other materials can create unique property profiles, making it a promising material for various applications. This research offers a rigorous analysis of the test statistic used by Johansen (2014) to identify common stochastic trends in a multivariate time series, under more broadened assumptions. Our study reveals that the critical value distribution converges to a specific limit case, which can be expressed through the use of ratio theorem. This theoretical framework provides the foundation for developing asymptotically valid p-values, an essential insight with implications. The new theory is capable of handling data sets with observations affected by heavy tails and differing sample sizes. The results show that the estimators for the number of common stochastic trends remain accurate and efficient, even in such challenging conditions. To verify the accuracy of our theoretical predictions, corresponding Monte Carlo simulations were conducted. Additionally, a step-by-step practical approach is proposed for determining the critical values, which is an invaluable tool for statistical analysis. The validity of our results is further confirmed through applications of the approach to three real-world data sets, encompassing the daily price movements of copper, the daily exchange rates of EURCHF, and the daily price movements of gold. The findings of our analysis include the identification of at least three common stochastic trends in the copper and gold price series, and at least four common stochastic trends in the daily exchange rates of EURCHF. Our results show that these series all possess a characteristic of co-movement observed in the price movements of copper, the daily exchange rates of EURCHF, and the commodity price index. On the other hand, the daily price movements of gold exhibit a distinct behavior differing from these other series. Our study explains this difference as a consequence of the observed cointegration patterns. Galaxy clusters acting as gravitational lenses create highly distorted, multiple-image systems. Recent research using high-resolution images has revealed the presence of small mass objects contributing to these distortions. We aim to explore the effectiveness of a neural network in identifying these small objects in a dataset comprising 11 galaxy clusters from the ALMA Fornax Survey. Using the smallest objects visible in Hubble F675W images as a reference, we trained and tested a convolutional neural network (CNN) to detect objects in both Hubble F675W and FMUV images. Our results show that the CNN successfully identifies objects in FMUV images, despite these having a coarser resolution than the Hubble images. We observed small objects in 8 out of 11 galaxy clusters, with some having multiple instances. Utilizing data from Hubble F675W and FMUV images combined allows us to detect a maximum of 279 probable small objects, implying they constitute approximately 25% of the mass required to explain substructure in galaxy clusters. These small objects are likely to be associated with star clusters, companions to lensing cluster galaxies, or unresolved star clusters within the field of view. Our study lays the groundwork for utilizing deep learning to identify small objects in future high-resolution wide-field surveys such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time. It also paves the way for a more precise estimation of the mass function of galaxy clusters by accurately accounting for substructure caused by small objects. Ultimately, understanding the mass function of galaxy clusters requires pinpointing the mass contributors – in this case, the numerous small mass objects we have identified. This study explores how a finite group of symmetries, G, affects a torus, T, when the group action involves periodic and equivariant properties. We use the techniques of algebraic and analytical calculations to determine the cohomology classes resulting from this action. Our findings reveal that the equivariant cohomology classes can be represented by twists, which are properties defined by G-invariant loops on the torus. The results are presented in a comprehensive format that includes the relationship between cohomology and twist spaces under various group actions, including those situations where the group action lacks periodic properties. By applying Borel's work on Betti numbers, we reconstruct the results for actions lacking periodic properties and establish an invariant, dim(H^*(T^2,G)), which represents the number of twist components under a given group action. Our study also identifies the conditions under which there exist non-trivial twist components with a dimension greater than one. To verify some of these conditions, we utilize molecular geometry to create 3D visual representations of torus surfaces displaying interesting and complex patterns. These patterns are a reflection of the intricate structures of equivariant cohomology spaces. Ultimately, our research leads to the discovery of various unusual and unique patterns resulting from the actions of finite groups on the torus, including patterns resembling chicken skin, probability distributions, rainbow colors, and radial/symmetric patterns. These visual representations highlight the complexity and intricacy of the equivariant cohomology spaces and serve as a testament to the beauty and significance of the algebraic and analytic calculations underlying these group actions. Our research also inspires future studies on the actions of finite subgroups within larger algebraic and geometric theories. As a byproduct of our research, we have created an online collection of interactive 3D visualizations, which can be accessed through our website. The collection includes a diverse range of torus surfaces displaying different patterns resulting from the actions of various finite subgroups on the torus. Our hope is that these visualizations will not only facilitate a deeper understanding of the algebraic and analytic results but also inspire future studies and contributions in this field. Our research is part of an ongoing project, called "Visual Insights into Symmetry," which aims to explore the intricate patterns resulting from the actions of finite subgroups on various geometric surfaces and shapes. Using a cone-like model, we studied the stability of the shock front in supernovae explosions, particularly the inner shock that forms when a massive star collapses. Our analysis focused on fast instabilities that occur when the star explodes, and we found that successful explosions lead to higher instability rates than failed explosions. This trend holds true for both outer and inner shocks. However, the inner shock tends to be more unstable than the outer shock. Our study considered a massive star with a specific mass and found that instabilities typically develop within a few seconds after explosion, and their occurrence is more likely at lower electron scattering depths. Our findings may help explain previously observed phenomena, such as the early light curve of supernovae and the emission of gamma-rays. Our model is suitable for further study using more complex simulations and could be used to investigate other aspects of supernovae, such as the formation of circumstellar disks and the efficiency of energy conversion. Our code is available for public use. https://github.com/superfastincube/superfastincube. Our paper provides a comprehensive overview of the model and its results. Recent advancements in deep learning technology have led to significant progress in identifying ADHD through brain imaging, however the issue remains that high-precision training data is hard to acquire. Acronyms are prominent in written communication, with many being context-specific to particular fields or regions. They present a challenge for readers who are unfamiliar with them, and even cause difficulties for text analysis systems. To address this issue, this study contributes two key findings. Firstly, a proven approach is established for identifying and distinguishing acronyms from different contexts. Secondly, a substantial dataset is created with annotated acronyms, providing a valuable resource for further research. Experiments demonstrate that this method effectively identifies acronyms and accurately disambiguates them, particularly in large-scale datasets. This study's resources and methods can be applied broadly to handle the complex issue of acronyms in various written content. The dataset is made available for public use at https://github.com/amanbasu/sci-acronyms. Further research is suggested to tackle the problem of ambient acronyms, where clear context is absent. Instead, reliance on statistical patterns in larger corpora might offer a viable approach for their detection and disambiguation. As an alternative, systems could be designed to learn from labeled data or explicitly be trained to recognize acronyms from context-free positions within text. Ultimately, a comprehensive understanding of acronyms could be achieved by integrating context-based and ambient approaches. The proposed method represents a first step toward solving the broader problem of recognizing and interpreting text without reference to specific contexts. The second part of this research focuses on tackling the problem of ambient acronyms in a realistic setting by incorporating the partial context available to these systems. This is in line with prior studies that have explored the role of partial context in helping disambiguation. By combining the pros of both approaches, hybrid systems that blend top-down learning from labeled data and bottom-up learning from partial context may offer the most promising solutions to the general problem of interpreting text in the absence of complete context. Thus, a valuable relationship was established between the two related problems of interpreting text both with and without complete context. We propose a theoretical framework for heat management in quantum Hall systems, focusing on the interaction between counter-propagating edge modes. The approach involves incorporating a local charge imbalance to establish a temperature gradient, similar to the function of thermal rectifiers. The theory is applied to the quantum Hall effect on graphene and GaAs heterostructures, with predicted results matching experimental outcomes. The framework's versatility allows for adaptation to other quantum systems, enabling the investigation of heat transport and the potential creation of novel heat devices. Moreover, we outline the requirements for laboratory measurement and analysis of the proposed phenomenon.

To write reliable DNA data, a DNA template is created by combining a forward and reverse primer pair. The template's storage capacity is limited because each primer pair can form a complete DNA molecule with a fixed tail, determining the amount of user data that can be encoded. The choice of primer design significantly affects the number of usable tiles, influencing how data are stored and retrieved from DNA storage systems. We developed a cutting tool for generating high-quality primers by modifying an existing DNA sequence to match user-provided data, utilizing a designed forward primer as a guide. This template can enhance DNA storage efficiency by expanding the usable sequence space, allowing multiple forward primers to produce comparable outcomes. Our proof of concept shows that this tool can boost the number of usable tiles per forward primer, demonstrating its potential to boost the overall storage capacity of DNA data storage systems. We show that this tool outperforms other DNA storage approaches and can achieve a large number of tiles per forward primer, approaching a maximum storage potential. The tool is now available as an open-source program. https://github.com/jaeyoun/prime-cut. An early version of this work was previously presented at IEEE Data Storage and Retrieval Workshop, 2020. https://doi.org/10.1109/DSRW2020-00112020.10001. A revised version was presented at ICDE 2021. https://ieeexploreiec.org/document/9411997/. A revised version was published in IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering, 2021. https://ieeexploreiec.org/document/9411997/. This letter introduces a novel method for efficient data retrieval based on DNA storage technology, utilizing a specialized tool. The tool modifies the DNA sequence to match a given data block, allowing for rapid identification of the corresponding forward primer. The tool generates high-quality primers by enhancing the usable sequence space, significantly outperforming existing DNA storage approaches. The tool demonstrates a substantial improvement in storage efficiency without decreasing the number of usable tiles per forward primer. We provide experimental results demonstrating the superior performance of our tool. The tool offers a groundbreaking solution for efficient DNA data retrieval. The tool is open-source for public use. https://github.com/jaeyoun/prime-cut. Distinct from other topological states (e.g., Weyl nodes, Dirac cones), 
nodal lines' topology is reflected in the Lie group structure of the momentum
space.  We illustrate that nodal lines in NCLSMs are generically one-dimensional

spaces.  Some prominent examples include topological nodal lines in trigonal
graphene,  nodal rings in hyperkagome lattice $\pi$-models,  and momentum
lines in twisted binary compounds.  We discuss that engineering the form of
nodal lines can grant control over a material's electronic structure, 
consequently its transport properties.  Precise analysis of the nodal lines
structure in the above mentioned materials shows that they feature anomalous
thermal transport characteristics due to the presence of a parameter-dependent
phonon drag effect.  The study of topological nodal lines' properties may
significantly advance our understanding of both conventional and unconventional
superconductors and their associated topological phases.

distinguish various superconducting topological phases.  Furthermore, we suggest

pairing states in superconductors,  characterized by nodal lines in the momentum
space that vary according to temperature.  Lastly,  we outline future avenues

semimetals and superconductors.  These investigations may provide crucial

This paper introduces a new method for estimating the entropy of a discrete-time Markov chain given partial access to its state space. Unlike previous approaches, our technique reassesses the information available to the observer and returns a maximum entropy estimate. This is particularly important because any viable entropy estimation algorithm requires the amount of information available to the observer to be greater than zero. By refining the input entropy problem, our solution yields more accurate estimates than existing methods. Using a grid search, we maximize the entropy subject to observational constraints and also develop conditions under which the optimal solution can be analytically derived. This approach is applied to a Berromean source, a Markov chain with unknown transition probabilities, and a Markov chain with mutually exclusive states, all utilizing symmetric blending and amortized inference methods. Simulations demonstrate that our entropy estimation algorithm outperforms traditional approaches. While this research primarily focuses on discrete-state Markov chains, the theoretical foundations can be applied to continuous-state chains by leveraging information measures and utilizing numerical methods for the state dimension. This is illustrated by a GPS trajectory example. Our code is available online for reproduction. This difficulty arises from the fact that deep learning models trained with synthetic data might not perform as well as human clinicians, who rely heavily on expertise. However, the benefit of using clinical features in data augmentation can vary based on the specific application, such as a simple binary model, where having clinical features might hinder performance. We explored the impact of including clinical information on data augmentation methods in predicting specific medical diagnoses. Our experiments involved creating a new dataset consisting of images and clinical information for two common inner ear conditions, and using this dataset to test the performance of augmented training, such as adding clinical information to the training process. Polymatroidal ideals have varied geometric interpretations, with deep connections to Hawkes processes, algebraic torus extensions, and sparse matrix representations. We find that the complement of these ideals' varieties is always covered by an algebraic torus. This phenomenon is equivalent to the quotient of a polynomial ring by a polymatroidal ideal exhibiting toric-dimensional regularization. We present specific criteria that ensure the smoothness of this torus and calculate its dimension. This research provides a method to recursively apply this result to more complex polymatroids. For linear polymatroids, we show that the described torus is a toric fiber bundle over a projective space, with a fiber that corresponds to a Hawkes process. This relationship is illustrated through examples. Our study of polymatroidal ideals offers a new perspective on toric-dimensional regularization and provides insight into the geometry of sparse matrix representations. Conversely, we may apply this perspective to analyze the underlying geometry of Hawkes processes. Additionally, we find that the proposed torus is a key component in establishing that the variety defined by a polymatroid's hyperplane arrangement has a nonempty intersection with every linear polymatroid. This result can be interpreted as a statement about the existence of sparse, full-rank matrices. We complement this finding with a new characterization of polymatroids based on their matroid structure, which is itself supported by an independent set of linear constraints. This characterization implies that the defined variety is a blow-up of the toric line segment that corresponds to the scalar multiples of the standard basis vectors in the polymatroid. This research offers various future research directions. For instance, it remains to be determined whether the described torus is always smooth, whether its dimension can be minimized, or whether the defined map to the polymatroid variety is a toric fiber bundle. Furthermore, we seek to establish a geometric relationship between the variety defined by a polymatroid and the Hawkes process itself, rather than just its fiber. Lastly, we explore the applicability of our methods to the broader class of ultramatic ideals, which encompasses polymatroidal ideals. We demonstrate that the defined torus is not necessarily sparse with respect to the ultramatic ideal when it is a linear polymatroid, unless the underlying matrix representing the polymatroid has a specific property, which is to have rank equal to its size minus one. We've developed a quantum version of the K-means clustering algorithm, using quantum circuits to achieve faster data processing. In the standard K-means method, data points are iteratively assigned clusters based on the nearest centroid, with the centroids updated accordingly. However, this algorithm has a significant shortcoming: it has an exponential time complexity of O($\sqrt{N}$) for large datasets, making it impractical. Our quantum algorithm utilizes a hybrid approach, combining classical and quantum computation to improve efficiency. By preprocessing data classically and using it in a quantum gradient circuit, we can reduce the complexity to O($d^3$), where $d$ is the number of features in the data, and $N$ is the number of data points. We've also introduced two variants of the algorithm, one that uses less qubits and another that requires fewer operations, both achieving a reduced time complexity of O($\theta^3$). When possible, we've incorporated fully quantum solutions, leading to a further improvement in complexity. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of solving clustering problems with a linear-scale number of operations, even with a large number of data points. This research opens up the possibility of using quantum computing for big data applications. To implement our algorithm, we've used the Qiskit framework and simulated the effects of qubit decoherence on the outcomes. Our results show promising signs for the potential of quantum computing to solve clustering problems, and we've provided the code for the simulations and algorithms on GitHub. Additionally, we've discussed the challenges and limitations of using quantum computing for clustering problems. Our research suggests that fully quantum approaches may be more suitable when data points are few, but classical methods remain a better choice for large datasets. Moreover, for smaller datasets, the trade-off between the number of qubits required and the efficiency of the algorithm needs to be considered. We suggest an efficient approach to render complex computer graphics with the aid of cloud computing. This method leverages parallel processing capabilities of cloud servers and eliminates the need for additional infrastructure to handle graphics processing. By redistributing complex graphics tasks across multiple cloud servers, the burden on users is significantly reduced. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method on shadow and reflection rendering, providing a more feasible alternative to traditional 3D ray tracing. Furthermore, our method facilitates the division of work among cloud servers and enables the allocation of computing resources based on the size and complexity of graphics tasks. The proposed shadow computation method comprises two main stages: distributing the shadow map task among cloud servers and combining the resulting maps. We outline the step-by-step process of this method and provide sample estimates of data transmission quantities. Moreover, we explore potential applications of this method in other graphics tasks. To showcase the efficacy of this method, we create a simple demo using Google Collaboratory's GPU environment and conduct a case study on shadow computation. We studied the stability of synchronized patterns in large systems of coupled oscillators with a common nonlinear signal. The effect of weak but nontrivial frequency dispersion on these stable patterns was examined using both mathematical modeling and laboratory experiments involving coupled pendulons. Our research found that this form of dispersion often reduces the size of the stable pattern area, contrary to its behavior in full dispersion. The theoretical model used to study this phenomenon was based on a simple oscillator equation describing periodic motions, and our results contribute to a better understanding of stable synchronization patterns in complex systems. These findings have implications for studying stability in systems that experience various forms of dispersion, and our experiments provide a concrete example of this effect in a real-world scenario. The combination of nonlinear signal management and weak frequency dispersion played a crucial role in identifying stable synchronization patterns, and our method could be applied to other complex systems where these factors are present. Moreover, the study of stable synchronization patterns can offer valuable insights into identifying and controlling periodic motions in large systems of coupled oscillators. The presence of multiple frequency oscillations in these patterns further adds to their complexity, and their behavior may not be captured through linear approximation analysis. By phaseshifting the oscillator signal, we were able to investigate how stable pattern areas change and how they can be influenced by modifying the phase difference. The study of stability in large systems of coupled oscillators has many practical applications, and our research provides a useful framework for understanding the effects of frequency dispersion and phase difference on stable synchronization patterns. The combination of theoretical modeling and experimental studies of coupled pendulons allows us to explore the dynamic behavior of stable synchronization patterns in a comprehensive manner. The results of our research can be applied to control periodic motions in large systems of coupled oscillators, and the role of phase difference and frequency dispersion in stabilizing synchronous states needs to be further explored. Angela Bates and I created a hybrid method for producing random uniform spanning trees. This new approach blends the best aspects of both a straightforward generator and one using a detailed exact algorithm, and our tests indicate that it generates these trees significantly faster. Notably, this speed boost remains consistent, even when the number of trees being generated is relatively small. Our data also suggest that the hybrid method outperforms the other two approaches in terms of the accuracy of its estimated asymptotic tree size. While our initial analysis is centered on the specific model of uniform spanning trees found on graphs that represent random walks on a tree-like structure, we believe that the general concept of our hybrid method could be applicable to a broader range of graph-related problems. In addition to our work on uniform spanning trees, I provide a straightforward implementation of this hybrid method, along with a more general solution for sampling a random spanning tree in a broader class of graphs, and then demonstrate how this solution can be adapted to address the "friendship forest" problem. Music representation learning has experienced significant growth, thanks in part to cross-modal retrieval tasks. Currently, available music datasets are insufficient to support high-performance music-text retrieval models. To address this limitation, we present the MusicTM-Dataset, a vast music-text collection with over 180,000 title-database pairs from Musescore, that includes over 72 million music sheets and 108,000 song lyrics. Experimental evaluations on four public datasets, including the MusicTM-Dataset, demonstrate the exceptional performance of our proposed music-text retrieval method. Moreover, our study showcases the MusicTM-Dataset's potential for generic music representation learning tasks via a range of experiments. We provide a framework for one-dimensional dark solitons on a plane that travel at a variable speed. This solution is modeled as $u_{II}(x,v,t)$ with the black soliton being a special case when the speed is exactly the soliton's topological speed $c$. Our goal is to show that using a certain transformation, the stability of the black soliton can be determined by proving the orbital stability of the dark soliton for all relevant speeds $v$. Moreover, the stability of the dark soliton is found to be conditionally robust when its speed $v$ is outside a specific range. This result implies that the stability of the black soliton is conditional, occurring only when its speed is within a narrow range or exactly the soliton's topological speed. Our approach to analyzing these traveling dark solitons is unprecedented and allows us to study their behavior, explaining certain phenomena observed in the Maxwell-Bloch system. Our findings also provide explanations for recently reported findings such as the existence of singular solutions and system dynamics. Our work also reveals the existence of system-bound states, known as system solitons, which are found to be stable and occur near the boundary of the stable range for the individual soliton. Our research is likely to expand into the study of higher-dimensional dark solitons that travel at variable speeds. We introduce an efficient approach for real-time collaborative planning, incorporating multiple guidance strategies in a unified manner. The implementation is based on the Lotse library, which provides optimized polynomial predictions within a specified radius. We develop a quadratic programming formula to calculate the initial thrust required for each strategy, taking into account the limitations of the vehicle's engines. The quad-programming solution is applied to a Walloon P-42 rocket, subject to engine bounds. A real-time capable solver is utilized to demonstrate the feasibility of our approach for online calculations. The proposed methodology is adaptable to various guidance techniques and can be integrated with different optimization methods. It is primarily designed for applications where coordinated maneuvers involving multiple strategies are necessary, such as hybrid trajectories with phase transitions and uplinks from celestial bodies. The approach presents a versatile solution for such complex scenarios, demonstrating a ~3fold improvement over a basic Euler integration method in terms of single-step accuracy. The resulting trajectory exhibits improved precision, ultimately achieving a maximum error of ~0.7 meters after 10 seconds of flight time. The proposed methodology exhibits fast computation times, with processing speeds of ~0.5 milliseconds that enable real-time applications. The numerical examples illustrate the efficacy of our approach, showcasing its suitability for real-time collaborative planning and its potential for expansion to hybrid multi-phase trajectories. The CNSYS detector is uniquely designed to measure two parameters - temperature and fast neutron flux. This is achieved by combining the properties of proton resonance in different materials, which is sensitive to temperature changes. In this study, the theoretical foundations of the CNSYS detector are re-examined by focusing on the temperature-dependent properties of the proton resonance, which actually provides an advantage in measuring temperature. The study also highlights the potential of the CNSYS detector to measure temperature in extremely high-flux environments, such as in fast neutron facilities. In addition, the study confirms that the CNSYS detector can effectively distinguish between heat generated by neutrons and external heat sources. In practical applications, the CNSYS detector has been successfully used to measure temperature and flux in the High Flux Isotope Reactor at Oak Ridge National Laboratory and in the MBIR reactor at the INET. The study also includes detailed analysis of the systematic errors and uncertainties associated with each measurement. The results of these applications demonstrate that the CNSYS detector is well-suited for high-precision temperature and flux measurements in research reactors. In particular, the CNSYS detector offers a unique advantage of directly measuring temperature and flux simultaneously with high accuracy, which reduces the measurement time and increases the productivity of experimental samples in research reactors. The study concludes with future plans for the CNSYS detector, which include enhancing its performance by incorporating advanced digital and micro-electromechanical system technology to measure temperature and flux in even greater detail. The revised CNSYS detector is expected to provide higher resolution and sensitivity, and could potentially be used in portable radiation detection applications. We have developed a theoretical framework, rooted in mean-field theory, for analyzing the behavior of a dilute gas composed of $N$ distinct species ($N \leq 99$) that interact through repulsive potentials, either hard-sphere or soft-sphere. This multi-component gas is being studied as it undergoes condensation into any number of distinct phases ($Q \leq N$). Our results reveal that, when parameters such as density and temperature are fixed and only the number of species is altered, there is a direct relationship between the number of possible condensates and species, with the gas exhibiting more complex condensation behaviors as the number of species increases. These high-dimensional systems, characterized by multi-component condensation, exhibit extensive properties that increase proportionally with the number of species. Our theoretical approach combines analytical calculations and a numerical resolution of the Gross-Mane-Sawatzki equations via a global search method. These techniques allow us to accurately determine the phase boundaries, extent of condensation, and molecular properties throughout the phase diagram of binary, tertiary, and quaternary gases. Our theoretical framework represents a high-dimensional extension of the well-established Lee-Huang-Yang theory, originally developed for binary gases. Our analysis accounts for short-range correlation effects in the gas, with the results showing a notable increase in the extent of condensation as the number of species increases from two to three, but relatively little change with additional species beyond three. Our findings will provide a framework for further research in the condensed matter and cool astrophysics fields. They will also offer a starting point for exploring the condensation behaviors of species groups within super-Earth planets. Our methodology, built on a combination of mean-field theory, analytical calculations, and global optimization, can be adapted for studying higher-dimensional systems, such as those formed by metal alloys, with the potential for scaling these studies up to even more complex systems. Our method may also be applied in the simulation of the formation of dust grains in stars. The Madsen-Weiss theorem can be interpreted as a form of the b-principle, with stability theorems serving as a type of corollary that applies universally. This comparison encourages the exploration of b-principle implementations through the use of mapping class group representations. Specifically, the theorem's core idea is reinterpreted in terms of the relative Madsen-Weiss theorem, which is then coupled with additional tools to derive a cellular version of the theorem. This cellular model forms the foundation for an algorithmic approach to solving folding problems. By extending the domain of application of the b-principle to cases involving non-orientable surfaces, a new method for solving folding problems is developed, which is demonstrated through its application to an explicitly stated problem. This novel solution sheds light on the relationship between the Madsen-Weiss theorem and the widely studied Morita-Mumford classification of representations of mapping class groups. Furthermore, the reimplementation of fundamental components of the Madsen-Weiss algorithm in terms of b-principle-based methods reveals that these components can be incorporated into a broader algorithm that solves a b-principle formulation of the generic double mapping class group. This latter group's structure is known to be rational and solvable, providing a new avenue for analyzing the computational complexity of algorithmic versions of the Madsen-Weiss algorithm. Lastly, the theoretical framework of b-principles is used to propose a new, more efficient version of the Madsen-Weiss algorithm. This proposed approach promises significant computational benefits, potentially leading to a significant reduction in the runtime of algorithmic implementations of the Madsen-Weiss theorem. This new method could potentially revolutionize the field by enabling the efficient calculation of universal abelian lifts of generic mapping class groups. If successful, this could pave the way for a computationally efficient derivation of the stable form of the Madsen-Weiss theorem. This innovative approach may also yield insights into the topological properties of development spaces, facilitating a new level of geometric analysis of the structure of these spaces, possibly even uncovering a new geometric relationship between the points of the Teichmüller space and the development spaces themselves. Consequently, this b-principle-based method of solving folding problems could have far-reaching implications for the geometric topology community by enabling the precise examination of the topological properties of development spaces.
