This study showcases that the representation capabilities of a point cloud registration network can be utilized for object classification. Unlike conventional approaches that train separate models for different tasks, our method trains a single model to both align point clouds and extract features. These features can then be leveraged across various object classification tasks. To achieve this, we developed a unified framework for aligning point clouds and performing object classification. This framework trains a single model on multiple datasets, allowing the model to learn feature representations that are transferable across datasets. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, with comparable or better performance than dedicated models on various object classification tasks. Moreover, we highlight the potential of our method to augment traditional object classification models with new capabilities, such as the ability to classify objects from unseen viewpoints. Our code is publicly available on GitHub. https://github.com/xtiangang1996/Unified Registration and Classification.

The conventional pipeline for instance segmentation involves a two-stage process. Initially, objects within an image are detected and pinpointed through a series of bounding boxes. Subsequently, these detected areas are subjected to mask generation. Although this method is widely adopted, it does come with a added complexity of second-pass processing, which can be cumbersome and expand computational requirements. In response to these limitations, we introduce a more integrated approach, CySGAN, that streamlines instance segmentation within a single unified framework. By integrating a cylinder-shaped spatial generator and concurrent object detection and masking processes, CySGAN effectively simplifies the pipeline while enhancing performance. Thorough experiments conducted across various metrics and benchmarks confirm the superior performance of CySGAN when compared to conventional methods. Notably, we observe a significant increase of 3.27% in the mAP metric for the COCO 2017 dataset. Action anticipation is crucial for predicting what's going to happen next in a sequence of human actions. Recent advancements in action sequences modeling have made significant strides in addressing this issue. Nonetheless, they primarily rely on linear interactions between past actions and future annotations, which is inadequate for capturing the complex, non-linear interactions often present in the data. To address this limitation, we propose a novel action anticipation model that leverages kernel methods to anticipate actions in a non-linear manner. The model's novel feature is that it treats past actions as inputs to a kernel function, which in turn enables the model to anticipate both discrete and continuous future actions based on a kernel-trained similarity matrix. We test the model's performance under different kernel specifications, including when it draws from real-world data distributions, as well as when it draws from a synthetic dataset specifically designed to mimic human motion patterns. The model's performance surpasses that of a basic support vector machine in both scenarios. Furthermore, when applied to the CMU Panoptic Action Dataset, the model's performance matches or exceeds state-of-the-art methods. To facilitate future research, the model, data, and source code are publicly available at https://github.com/acharyadeb2/Anticipating-Actions. Although Leibniz's view of infinity has been extensively examined, his actual meaning of 'infinitesimal' and 'infinity' remains disputed. Historians of mathematics and philosophy have varied in their understanding of Leibniz's infinity, often presenting it as a philosophical rather than a mathematical concept. What is more, his views on bounded and unbounded infinity have been recognized as significant yet underexplored aspects of his intellectual legacy. This paper aims to redress this oversight by examining the various ways Leibniz's concepts of bounded and unbounded infinity have been interpreted. It specifically looks at the early, middle, and late periods of Leibniz's life and how his views on bounded and unbounded infinity were received by other thinkers such as Clarke, Wolff, and Berkeley. By conducting a thorough analysis, this paper aims to clarify the distinct meanings of bounded and unbounded infinity and their relationships to the continuum, as well as to identify potential areas for further research into Leibniz's concept of infinity. It is found that Leibniz's concept of bounded infinity has often been overlooked in favor of his unbounded infinity, although it holds significance as a philosophical and intellectual heritage that deserves more attention. Moreover, while his unbounded infinity has been variously seen as a metaphysical, ontological, or cosmological concept, the meaning of bounded infinity remains more ambiguous and in need of further investigation. As a whole, this paper aims to enhance our understanding of Leibniz's complex and intricate intellectual legacy, which continues to warrant continued research and reflection. Additionally, this paper briefly explores some of the far-reaching effects of Leibniz's concept of bounded and unbounded infinity on later thinkers such as Kant, Swinburne, and Meyerson. It is found that while Kant's view of the infinite may seem diametrically opposed to Leibniz's, their positions on bounded infinity are surprisingly aligned. What is more, an analysis of the concept of bounded infinity reveals a less well-known affinity between Leibniz and these three late modern philosophers. Despite their significant differences over the nature of reality and morality, these thinkers' engagement with Leibniz's concept of bounded infinity reveals a remarkable continuity of thought. It is hoped that this research will stimulate fresh perspectives on the later periods of the Scientific Revolution and the Enlightenment, as well as on the ongoing research into Leibniz's intellectual legacy. A powerful technique for observing the cosmic microwave background has been developed using ground-based surveys and optical/infrared cameras. To identify the linear polarization signature of the CMB, the signal is typically processed against a model of the foreground environment. This model is created through the analysis of galactic data and used to remove foreground contamination. The effectiveness of the foreground removal method is essential; if the approximation of the foreground model is poor, it can jeopardize cosmological parameter estimation. To assess the impact of imperfect foreground removal, we applied a Bayesian parameter estimation approach to simulated CMB polymers and fractional polarization maps, and examined the effects of remaining foreground contaminants on parameter estimation. We found that even with the simplified foreground model used in this study, the estimated fractional polarization signature of the CMB was accurate to within 5% for key parameters. When more realistic fractional polarization maps were employed, the error margin decreased to less than 2%. Notably, we observed that the estimated scale of the CMB polymers was less precise, with a margin of error exceeding 50% even in the most optimized scenario. This analysis emphasizes the significance of accurate foreground removal in observational CMB polarization studies and highlights the need for improved modeling of the galactic foreground environment. Additionally, we identified and reviewed the currently available tools for optical foreground removal. While these tools performed relatively well in this study, we believe further advancements can be achieved through the integration of machine learning techniques. Finally, we provide recommendations for the development of future CMB polarization foreground removal methods, suggesting that a modular and adaptable structure would enable easy updates and enhancements as new data becomes available. This is particularly crucial for ongoing and planned ground-based CMB polarization experiments that will increasingly rely on accurate foreground removal methods to achieve their scientific objectives. Based on our analysis, we propose a multi-layered and versatile optical foreground removal pipeline, named POLCA, which we believe will effectively serve the needs of such experimental programs. This pipeline is designed to incorporate multiple removal methods, facilitate the integration of new data, and allow for the customization of foreground models to suit the unique requirements of specific CMB polarization surveys and cosmological analyses. By adopting POLCA as a standardized and versatile tool, we aim to ensure the accurate elimination of galactic foreground contamination, thereby enabling a deep exploration of the cosmic microwave background's statistical and cosmological properties. This includes the fractional polarization signature of the CMB and potentially other intriguing phenomena such as CMB polymers. We analyze various aspects of operators that maintain linear independence when applying them to sequences of vectors. Specifically, we define a bounded operator $T$ on a Hilbert space $H$ such that any given finite group of operators that commute with $T$ does not destroy the linear independence of sequences. Our findings indicate that $T$ must be a scalar multiple of the identity operator, with the scalar being unique and constant for the operator's spectrum. We also explore related conditions and examine the implications of more stringent independence criteria, ultimately gaining insight into the operator's properties when the underlying space has a rich structure. Our study includes examples and illustrations to facilitate understanding. Additionally, we discuss how these results are connected to certain problems and research areas within complex analysis and operator theory. One such connection led us to develop a new concept, which we then utilize to identify necessary and sufficient conditions for preserving linear independence when applying a family of operators. This leads us to introduce the notion of a relatively compact operator set and to identify essential criteria for this property, thereby gaining insight into the operator's behavior, especially when the operators are compact or have certain spectral properties. Our findings are further refined in the case of Euclidean spaces, where the properties of translation-invariant linear independence and compactness can be completely elucidated. This led us to identify essential characteristics of translation-invariant compact operator sets, which we then use to resolve a problem connected to the operator's spectrum. One of our key findings is that the relatively compact operator set is equivalent to a compact operator when the underlying space has a rich structure. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this relationship does not hold in the case of Euclidean spaces, where the properties of relatively compact and compact operator sets differ significantly. Our study also enabled us to identify and characterize the properties of compact operator sets that are translation-invariant, as well as relatively compact sets, which encompass a range of important and distinct properties. For instance, we found that a relatively compact operator set that is translation-invariant is always compact, but this inverse relationship does not hold in the case of Euclidean spaces. By examining the properties of relatively compact and compact operator sets, we gained valuable insight into the relationships between these concepts, as well as the properties of relatively compact and compact sets, which are often utilized in the study of Poincaré's inequality and the properties of certain differential operators. This led us to identify and characterize the properties of relatively compact and compact operator sets in a new context, as well as tight closure, which is a crucial concept in this area

Various document modeling techniques have been employed to enhance various recommender systems, resulting in substantial improvements. This success, however, remains largely disconnected from theoretical co-occurrence-based model developments. This study bridges this gap, introducing a new document model that integrates theoretical co-occurrence-based findings to capture latent document patterns. We derive a novel generative model and propose two corresponding maximum likelihood estimation algorithms. The resulting model outperforms current best practices in two real-world scenarios, as demonstrated by our experiments. Additionally, our analysis shows that prior methods were likely driven by latent topic structures present within the data. We also conduct an in-depth examination of how individual document model components contribute to recommendation accuracy and find that the payoffs are somewhat nuanced. Overall, our work highlights the potential of theoretically grounded document models to boost recommendation accuracy, especially in data-sparse environments. The optimal selection of these parameters enables the instrument to operate at its standard speed, while poorer choices may slow it down by up to threefold.  The findings suggest that a limited set of suitable stabilization parameter combinations is available for the GRAVITY camera, allowing for a maximum of four distinct modes of operation.  To facilitate a more efficient gain evaluation, it is recommended to activate the Fast Switcher only when the signal amplification is uncertain, thereby reducing the time required for this assessment. We investigate a probabilistic approach to solving linear systems of polynomials, allowing for a limited number of errors. Focusing on polynomial degrees d and h, we establish a threshold below which a solution to a system of polynomials of degree d, given v(h-1)v(h+1)...v(n+1), can be found by conducting at most O((log N)^O(1)) many evaluations, where v(j) can be any of v(j-1), j(v(j-1)), or a random linear combination of v(j-1), with associated verification steps requiring O(dn) computations. This evaluation count matches the deterministic result of Schaub et al. and represents an improvement over previous probabilistic results. Additionally, we present an algorithm for solving errors in linear systems of polynomials in O((log N)^O(1)) many evaluations, where each evaluation, either in solving or verifying, results in a random antipodal perturbation of the input system. This algorithm uses approximate greatest common divisors, as well as an innovative method for solving error-laden polynomial systems of degree d over a field, involving a parameter that controls the number of errors, in O(nd + n^2) many evaluations. We also explore applications of these findings, including converting certain forms of privacy to privacy over infinite datasets, utilizing random answers to mask sensitive data, and protecting privacy in the presence of evasive data. These applications were not covered in the associated code provided on arXiv, but will instead be addressed in a companion paper. Seminal work by Ge, Bonnetain, and Iwanami provides a more recent probabilistic solution to linear system solving, which we build upon to derive our current results. We have developed a novel approach that enables the independent manipulation of dual-photon emission, including matched and mismatched pairs, from a two-level atom interacting with a resonant electromagnetic field. By applying a hybrid time-control method that combines $\sigma_{\pm}$ Rabi oscillations, we achieve complete control over the emission of individual photons. This strategy includes maximizing emission, suspension of emission, reversal of photon direction, and interconversion of matched and mismatched correlations. Notably, we find that this technique is efficient despite the limitations imposed by excited state effects and cavity decay. Our findings illustrate the potential of using a single control beam to fully regulate multi-photon emission through the combination of Rabi oscillations and Rabi flops. This approach may find applications in the generation of complex light states, quantum information encoding, and controlled photon transfer. The JUNO experiment is an underground neutrino observatory constructed at a site known for its low background interference in China. By utilizing large and sensitive photomultiplier detectors capable of gathering numerous signal events, JUNO's experiment aims to provide high-accuracy measurements of astrophysical neutrino events originating from various sources such as supernovae, neutron stars, and gamma-ray bursts. Furthermore, the experiment is designed to offer insights into neutrino oscillation patterns. To achieve these goals, the JUNO experiment features 20,000 pmTs, covering an area of 22.5 kt and capable of registering low-energy neutrino interactions as far as 100 km. By leveraging an innovative selection algorithm, which effectively filters out background interference, the experiment can isolate low-energy events and provide precise measurements of astrophysical neutrino spectra. To tackle the noted background issue at the site, the experiment employs an exterior liquid scintillator anti-neutrino detector, known as ALPINE, which utilizes 27 kt of active scintillator and 259 pmTs to detect high-energy neutrino interactions as far as 100 km. By collaborating with the GLASS and TREXINE neutrino oscillation experiments, the JUNO project gains valuable expertise in detector construction, data acquisition, and analysis, ultimately contributing to the advancement of neutrino research. To address concerns regarding the experiment's sensitivity to high-energy astrophysical neutrino events, the project is working on an enhanced strategy to minimize background interference, which will enable the detection of nearly 25% more events than previously anticipated. By leveraging this robust approach, the JUNO experiment is poised to offer repeatable, consistent results for neutrino oscillation patterns, as well as the most accurate low-energy astrophysical neutrino spectrum measurements to date. To facilitate the detection of rare high-energy neutrino events, the project is developing an advanced machine learning algorithm to refine existing selection methods, which show notable promise in enhancing the experiment's overall capabilities. By optimizing the experiment's overall performance, the JUNO project is close to achieving the world's best results for: (1) measuring the lightest neutrino mass, (2) distinguishing between different neutrino mass ordering, (3) detecting low-energy astrophysical neutrino events, and (4) detecting rare high-energy neutrino events beyond the current experimental limits. We introduce a novel ensemble method called Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) that capitalizes on the details provided by label distributions. PILE uses a pairwise approach to model log-odds calculations at both the class-level and instance-level, allowing it to learn from label information through an iterative process. By taking the gradient of the log-loss across adjacent classes, PILE ensures that the logits of neighboring classes are discriminatively separated. Additionally, by directly manipulating instance-level logits, PILE effectively handles label distributions with inherent ambiguities. Our experiments demonstrate PILE's effectiveness in tackling label ambiguity issues for multiple loss functions and various deep network architectures, yielding a notable improvement of at least 2% accuracy for the standard CIFAR-100 dataset and 10% for the AMIM dataset, which simulates label ambiguity. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/hudsonbeast/PILE.

Furthermore, we find that the performance of the network can be augmented by increasing its effective sensitivity and effective integration time. By comparing our results to current astronomical and gravitational wave experiments, we find that the frequencies targeted by current searches are not optimal for achieving the best possible sensitivity and accuracy. real-time events.

In situations where direct access to a probability distribution is not possible, its entropy must be estimated. Theoretical analysis and experimental findings indicate that low-bias approximations are not feasible in general, with their accuracy largely dependent on the level of data availability. When only partial access to the distribution is possible, the form of this access is also crucial: approximations based on samples or marginal information have different characteristics and consequences. To overcome these limitations, a novel approximation method is proposed, utilizing partial information in the form of marginal distributions. This method does not rely on assumptions and is based on maximizing entropy subject to given constraints. The theoretical foundations of this approach are laid out, and its performance compared to popular low-bias approximations through numerical experiments. Interestingly, it is shown that one common source of partial information - counting probabilities - can yield an accurate estimate of entropy. The proposed method is implemented as a freely available software package. The research presented has potential applications in information theory, probability, computer science, and statistical physics. Its practical relevance is demonstrated by its application to two real-world problems: estimating entropy from video comparisons, and measuring fine-grained statistical association in images. The software code and reproducible documentation are available online at public repositories. The validated results are presented in the appendix. Firstly, we leverage Borel measures to understand the distribution of states and fluxes within the system. Secondly, we derive a set of integral equations that describe the temporary and spatial changes in these measures. These equations enable us to identify general conditions for verifying stability in the system and to derive specific bounds on the stability threshold. Our methodology is applied to a simplified model of a semiconductor manufacturing system, which consists of three types of customers (units): job parts circulating through the system, additional parts generating jobs, and supervising parts controlling the system. Our analysis provides general criteria for checking stability in this complex system and offers specific upper and lower limits on the stability threshold. Our study culminates in the calculation of the exact stability threshold for a particular set of parameter values. Our analytical findings are illustrated through numerical examples. Furthermore, we verify the validity of asymptotic approximations for large values of the system parameters. As an additional application, we investigate the condition under which the system behaves as a classical M/M/2 queue. Our method is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of models with similar structures. Moreover, it can be modified to deal with more complex models featuring different types of customers. Finally, our analytical results are made available in a fully automated algorithm that can efficiently solve equilibrium measures and evaluate the stability threshold for a given system. To improve IoT security, precise identification of vulnerabilities is essential but deploying attack classifiers on devices with limited resources is challenging due to memory and computational constraints. Our NBcoded tool addresses this issue by providing a lightweight, adaptable, and efficient solution for classifying threats. NBcoded utilizes a modified version of Naive Bayes algorithm and translates trained models into readable, easy-to-understand decision trees, while minimizing memory usage. Additionally, NBcoded optimizes tree reductions and leverages binary encoding to further reduce memory requirements. This allows NBcoded to successfully classify vulnerabilities on devices with very limited resources, as demonstrated by our experiments. More information is available at: https://nbcoded.github.io/. The biological object detection uses a novel binary activation function to create cells that produce outputs with biological characteristics. We have tested our new technique on live cell images and compared its performance with traditional object detection methods, which are based on spatio-temporal information alone. The results have shown that our technique not only accurately identifies biological objects, but it also provides a more reliable feature for describing their movement. The implementation details can be found at our online repository https://github.com/hjzhou2016/BiologicalObjectDetection. To facilitate the community in using our technique, we have also provided a tutorial for biological movement analysis using a common programming language. As a result, our technique has successfully identified the movement patterns of living cells, which would otherwise be difficult to detect with existing image analysis methods. The discovery could provide valuable information about the functions of cells, such as those found in cancerous tumors. To our knowledge, our technique presents the first description of a new type of cell movement, which occurs in a common type of cell called fibroblast cells. As a result, this model is able to provide a more accurate understanding of how drag forces contribute to the objects' motion, and can also estimate the rate at which forces change with different variables. The effective taper section facilitates efficient emission of photons from the quantum dot into a surrounding waveguide, enhancing coupling efficiency while reducing feedback. Through finite-difference time-domain simulations, we found that a typical planar photonic crystal nanowire without a taper section yields a coupling efficiency of approximately 1% when the quantum dot is positioned at the end of the nanowire. Conversely, incorporating our optimized taper section and a stop gap at the end of the nanowire yields a coupling efficiency of about 99% for photons emitted within its structure. Furthermore, the design features a wide bandwidth, spanning over 20 nm, thereby accommodating diverse semiconductor material combinations and minimizing feedback into the quantum dot. We evaluated the performance of this design using the Green's tensor formalism and found that a quantum dot positioned within the taper section achieves high emission rates into the forward direction, low reversal rates, and a wide bandwidth compared to conventional designs. Additionally, the design can be enhanced to support multi-mode emission by increasing the size of the photonic crystal claddings. We applied the Green's tensor formalism to analyze single-photon emission properties such as correlation functions, spectrum, and efficiency in both conventional and optimized nanowire designs. The results show a substantial improvement in photon emission efficiency in the advanced taper section-based single-photon source compared to the basic planar photonic crystal nanowire design. The design we present will likely facilitate further advancements in the creation of on-chip single-photon sources utilizing semiconductor quantum dots. The developed taper section-based photonic crystal nanowire structure can also be adapted for detecting weak light signals emitted from quantum dots located near the focus of microscopes with a numerical aperture equivalent to the design's forward directional photon emission efficiency. Therefore, the innovative taper section-based photonic crystal nanowire structure holds great promise for microspectroscopy applications. Lastly, the design can be modified at the quantum dot position to enable efficient light emitted thereinto to reflect the incident polarized light, effectively enabling the complete elimination of Brillouin scattering, a significant source of noise in photonic devices, when using linear cavity enhancement techniques. However, in cases where multi-objective optimization doesn't suffice, using multimodal optimization can significantly increase the number of optimal solutions. Combining both approaches seems promising. We introduce a novel method called hybrid multimodal-multi-objective optimization (HMMO) and demonstrate its effectiveness using a modified version of the Janus function. HMMO's performance is compared to that of similar techniques and the results show that, depending on the problem at hand, this approach can be a valuable tool. Furthermore, Hybrid Big Bang-Janus Evolution (HBBJE) and Hybrid DE-Janus Evolution (HJDE) are proposed as two feasible implementation methods for HMMO. We develop theoretical and experimental foundations for these schemes and conduct comprehensive testing to evaluate their performance. The outcomes demonstrate that both methods are effective and can be employed to tackle complex optimization challenges. Notably, HBBJE and HJDE exhibit similar performance in most cases but sometimes differ slightly, with HBBJE sometimes outperforming HJDE can be attributed to its diverse search strategies. We've established a few core definitions and theorems related to clouds in metric space context. Our approach draws inspiration from Etienne Ghate's work but diverges from it in significant ways. Ghate defined a cloud as a set of points with shared stabilizer and demonstrated that such points lie near the center of their geometric embedding. However, Ghate's method relies on projective space concepts that are irrelevant in metric space context. Conversely, we focus on the core issue - the relationship between stabilizer and center in metric space context. Our key contribution is Theorem 3.4, which proves that a cloud with a non-trivial stabilizer must have a center that is isolated, a property distinct to convex subsets. Moreover, we've found that this property distinguishes clouds from other geometric subsets - our geometric subset is strictly inclusive of the convex subsets. Finally, we've found that this property is sufficient to characterize clouds; any subset with an isolated center will have a cloud projection onto it, which is geodesically convex and includes all points closest to that center. help machine learning models develop meaningful feature representations. By creating
a balanced mix of visual components, Bonsai generates a graphical structure
capturing the inherent relationships within the data. Interpreting the Bonsai
visualization as a hierarchical model, it reveals the underlying logical sequence
of feature extraction, from high-level categorical features to detailed numerical
characteristics. Furthermore, the hierarchical structure of Bonsai allows for
the discovery of new relationships among the data, facilitated by its graphical
interface that links features to their corresponding meanings. Inspired by the
conceptual similarities between this process and the practice of growing a Bonsai
tree, our method aims to cultivate a system that harmoniously integrates the
statistical analysis of data and the strategic planning of model functionality. We
demonstrate the efficacy of Bonsai through its application to a dataset from the
field of medicine, where we showcase its utility in identifying the core features
contributing to a model's accuracy. Additionally, we share our findings on the

This study investigates the properties of monolithic small collection-electroide CMOS sensors with a thin sensing layer, where charge collection occurs largely through the sensor's semi-conductive material. An analytical model and computer simulations utilizing the FINSIM program are employed to examine the influence of signal magnitude, signal duration, and sensor thickness on signal output. An experimental validation of the model is carried out using samples from the CMS TC17 project. The simulations reveal that increasing sensor thickness does not proportionally extend signal output duration due to reduced charge collection. As a result, shorter signal periods are produced for larger signals. This unique characteristic gives rise to the possibility of using a single analog signal processing method for signals of varying magnitudes. Furthermore, the model demonstrates accuracy in predicting signal output and matching experimental results for different signal durations and energies. An optional rectilinear signal shaping algorithm is also investigated, which reduces output signals to a single magnitude. The model, simulations, and experimental results consistently indicate that this shaping technique effectively eliminates signal magnitude as a factor. Finally, the model shows that thick sensor layers compromise its performance, underscoring the importance of accurately determining sensor thickness in precision monolithic sensors. An added benefit of this study's findings is the identification of a method for precisely determining sensor thickness based on charge collection characteristics. In turn, this technique can be employed to identify in-flight damaged regions within monolithic sensors incorporating a cantering structure. A damaged area is defined as a region with reduced charge collection efficiency. An in-depth analysis of a monolithic sensor's performance under various radiation levels is also conducted, as well as the implementation of a trigger shaping algorithm designed to conserve signal quality despite the presence of high levels of background noise. Lastly, the study verifies that its methodology and model remain accurate for trigger purposes up to an overall trigger efficiency of sixty percent. Moreover, the study found that its model's predictions and experimental results consistently agree across a wide range of noise levels. This achievement represents a major breakthrough in the field, as it presents a viable method for applying noise reduction techniques to monolithic sensors operating at high levels of activity and background noise. The goal of achieving 10e-16 flux ratio precision in exoplanet detection through direct image analysis has driven research into new techniques to support future large-scale ground-based telescopes. This paper introduces a novel approach called Field Formation Imaging (FFI), a new modality that complements existing data sets, such as sparse sampling techniques. FFI extends the principle of data collection to include spatial frequency information, allowing the use of any optical device to gather data. The paper outlines the theoretical basis for FFI and proposes a optimization method for signal recovery. This technique is tested using data from the Simple Fast Astro-Telelescope (SFAT), a device that conducts sine-wave plate tests, and is compared to results from ptychographic reconstruction and a regular grid-based reconstruction. The outcome shows that our technique surpasses these controls in precisely measuring signal flux and background noise. This improvement could enhance the performance of current 8-10 meter ground-based exoplanet detection systems by a factor of two to three. The application of FFI to large-scale interferometric systems holds great promise for detecting faint exoplanets, particularly those suitable for direct detection. The emergence of FFI could revolutionize the field, possibly leading to the discovery of smaller exoplanets and new planetary systems. The proposed approach is now being tested in a controlled environment at the Block Adaptive Optical (BAO) facility. If successful, this experiment will pave the way for the development of an innovative and flexible exoplanet detection device. We introduce a new stochastic hybrid asset-liability management model that balances cash flow risk and investment return objectives. The model dynamically switches between cash flow and investment strategies in response to market fluctuations and it adapts to negative interest rate environments. The cash flow component follows a discrete-time Markov chain that captures the volatility of cash reserves, leading to a stochastic differential equation representation of asset and liability values. The model then combines with investment strategies governed by mean-reverting jump processes, enabling the optimization of return and risk objectives subject to liquidity constraints. The optimization problem is solved using the conjugate gradient method and via a reinforcement learning approach with a neural network. The model's applicability extends to situations where interest rate models fail to account for non-negligible cash flow risk, such as during periods of pandemic-related crisis, and it is effective in portfolios dominated by euro-denominated instruments. This study addresses the issue of estimating cluster-conditional mean and variance in financial data, particularly when clusters have unequal sizes. Existing solutions heavy on assumptions will be contrasted with new, less assumption-dependent methods. Our novel estimators are initially tested in simulations, where they outperform other approaches, even in small sample sizes. Next, we apply and validate these new estimators using real-world financial data sets. One such application involves using our cluster-robust estimator to analyze the impact of corporate governance on financial characteristics. The analysis reveals significant differences in means and variances among the four categories of corporate governance, where means vary most and variances exhibit distinct patterns. Furthermore, the positive relationship between firm size and financial characteristics is more pronounced in well-governed firms, whereas the opposite is true for poorly governed firms. The findings provide new insights into the role of corporate governance in firm behavior. Moreover, the study demonstrates the effectiveness of our estimator in analyzing the effect of market liquidity on stock price movements, utilizing daily price data from the NYSE for one year. The results indicate that our estimator is robust even in small sample sizes, where it reduces standard errors by 23%, and reveals the presence of distinct cluster-conditional autocorrelation patterns. Lastly, the study employs our estimator to investigate the presence of distinct cluster-conditional autocorrelation patterns in daily exchange rate returns in the foreign exchange market. The results show that our estimator is robust even in very small sample sizes and exhibits less bias compared to existing solutions. Importantly, the evidence supports the presence of persistent autocorrelation patterns in pair-wise exchange rates up to 2 years, albeit with declining significance after 2 years. The findings provide new evidence on the behavior of foreign exchange markets. To facilitate practical application, the study makes its software publicly available on GitHub. To date, there are no other estimators that can handle the concurrent estimation of cluster-conditional mean and variance in small sample sizes as efficiently as our new approach. As a result, our approach offers valuable new insights for financial data analysis. Moreover, the study shows that our estimators reduce the bias in common financial metrics such as beta and return and volatility spreads by 34% and 13%, respectively. Consequently, our approach provides more accurate estimates that can enhance risk assessment and comparison between financial assets. We conducted a detailed study on how the choice of time steps affects the solution accuracy and stability, leading to the derivation of a stringent condition for maintaining numerical stability. Specifically, the absorption model of color dipole-gluon interaction, which treats the absorption process linearly, has been compared to a non-linear framework that accounts for the re-scattering effect. The magnitude of nuclear broadening, as observed in the forward hadron spectra of proton-lead collisions at the LHC, varies significantly between the two models. While the linear model predicts a gradual increase in nuclear broadening with respect to centrality, the non-linear model exhibits an initial increase followed by a decline at more peripheral events. Our analysis suggests that the ratio of nuclear broadening to geometric depletion, as obtained from the p-Pb collisions at the energies of the LHC, is largely insensitive to the choice of scale parameters governing the dipole cross section. Nonetheless, the preference for the non-linear model becomes apparent when considering the geometric hardence parameter governing the interaction between two dipoles. The implications of our findings on the measurement of parton saturation momentum are also discussed. Furthermore, our comparison between the linear and non-linear models of dipole cross section reveals that the preference for the non-linear model is largely unaffected by the uncertainties associated with the extraction of saturation momentum from data. Specifically, our comparison between the two models of dipole cross section shows that the difference in predictions for nuclear broadening is largely retained when accounting for the longitudinal motion of partons within the nucleus. Our comprehensive study on the linear and non-linear models of dipole cross section provides novel insights into the nuclear broadening observed in the forward hadron spectra of proton-lead collisions at the LHC. We explore various equivalence relations that emerge from models of continuous first-order logic. In particular, we investigate the properties of these equivalence relations in relation to ultrapowers of complete metric spaces within the context of continuous logic. Furthermore, we establish connections between these equivalence relations and isomorphism relations among structures comprised of complete metric spaces, and also within the context of category theory, drawing parallels with concepts associated with etale maps. Moreover, we introduce an notion of representability for subsets of metric spaces, and utilize this concept to separate the generic isomorphism relation from the equivalence relation corresponding to elementary equivalence. Finally, we demonstrate that the theory of continuous first-order logic does not admit quantifier elimination, unless the corresponding relativized theory excludes models with "dividing" actions on their residue fields. This finding contrasts with the situation in valued fields, where such a restriction leads to quantifier elimination. We also outline potential future directions for research, including drawing parallels between continuous logic and logic applied to locales, as well as investigating the notion of categoricity within the context of continuous logic. Moreover, we briefly discuss connections between functors representing germs of automorphism groups and the notion of definability in continuous logic. In addition, we establish that the functor representing the group action of the residue field can be expressed through a first-order theory. Conversely, we demonstrate that the theory associated with any non-trivial first-order class admitting a Galois categority can be expressed as the theory associated with the residue field action. Finally, we discuss how the notion of categoricity may be applied to problems related to algebraic geometry, such as determining whether certain subfields of algebraic type within arbitrary algebraically closed fields have non-trivial actions by automorphisms. In answering this question, we establish that the presence of an action by automorphisms on any field that is algebraic over a given field implies a corresponding equivalence relation that divides the isomorphism relation, and then demonstrate that the situation is non-trivial in the case of fields that are finite over a given field. This discovery leads us to conclude that the corresponding functor has a geometric interpretation, and subsequently, that the theory associated with any non-trivial first-order class admitting a Galois categority is equivalent to the theory associated with the action of the residue field being trivial. In a geometric context, this implies the presence of a non-trivial dynamical action on the projective line. This research develops a model for tracking line code changes across successive software updates. The objective is to utilize this model in identifying insertions, deletions, and rearrangements within software lines by comparing their current and previous states. We outline a method for managing software evolution through value preservation, utilizing the capabilities of singular value decomposition. This model is capable of detecting structural changes within software files by monitoring the distribution of values representing code line meanings. We present a technique for extracting a compressed representation of the distribution of codes' value densities, leveraging singular value decomposition. The approach involves treating distinct software versions as columns in a data matrix, and applying singular value decomposition to identify prevalent code characteristics. We manually verify the accuracy of the proposed method on ten diverse projects from GitHub, observing its effectiveness in detecting code rearrangements and preserving the essential information of the code's value distribution. The projects evaluated are Python-based, comprising: pyauto, gfy, llvmlib, pandas, pygmu, scipy, seal, sklearn, and torchDistribution. The results indicate that our method successfully identifies known code rearrangements from the projects analyzed. We calculate the preservation rate of the model for each project: pyauto (88.7%), gfy (99.9%), llvmlib (99.9%), pandas (99.9%), pygmu (99.9%), scipy (99.8%), seal (99.8%), sklean (99.9%), and torchDistribution (99.9%). The numerical data underlying this calculation is made available through our repository. The method reveals its potential in detecting structural changes within software files by showcasing its ability to distinguish the distinct evolution patterns of software lines. We present four cases where the method successfully identifies the unique distribution of code value densities across different software versions. The results indicate that singular value decomposition is a viable approach for managing software evolution while preserving the essential characteristics of the code's value distribution. The method demonstrates its effectiveness in detecting code rearrangments and maintaining the essential information of the code's value distribution across diverse projects. We make the code and data underlying this research freely available through our repository. Our team has observed the very powerful supernova remnant Cassiopeia A using the JAXA's Astro-X1 satellite. We analyzed the observations made on the 10th of June, 2019, which spanned from hard X-rays of 5-30 keV, to reveal their connection with massive cosmic rays. We found that the X-rays emitted from the north-eastern part of the remnant correlated strongly with the local magnetic field, as inferred from radio observations. We measured the angle between the polarization of the X-rays and the local magnetic field to be approximately 45 degrees. We also discovered that the X-rays emitted from the western part of the remnant are polarized in a direction opposite to the local magnetic field, which is thought to be caused by the acceleration of electrons by the magnetic field. We used the observed polarization to estimate the degree of polarization of high-energy gamma-rays emitted from the remnant, which are thought to be produced by the interaction of accelerated particles with the magnetic field. We found that the degree of polarization of the gamma-rays is likely to be significant, which could be as high as 10% or more. We also used the observed polarization to study the geometry of the local magnetic field, as well as the mixing of accelerated particles within the remnant. We calculated that the ratio of low to high energy gamma-rays emitted from the north-eastern part of the remnant is likely to be significant, which could be as high as 0.1. We also discovered that the observed emission from the western part of the remnant is consistent with the interaction of accelerated particles with the magnetic field. We used the observed emission to estimate the rate of injection of particles into the magnetic field, which is likely to be significant. We compared our findings with simulations of the emission from the plasma and found that the observed emission is likely to be partially explained by the simulation. However, the simulated emission falls short of explaining the observed rate of injection of particles into the magnetic field. We also used the observed emission to study the mixing of accelerated particles within the remnant. We found that the particle distribution within the remnant at 125 years after the explosion is likely to be more even than previously thought. Furthermore, we used the observed emission to study the local magnetic field. We found that the local magnetic field in the north-eastern part of the remnant is likely not to be the primary source of acceleration. We also used the observed emission to study the local density of the gas within the remnant.

This research explores the phenomenon of smooth counting, a concept first introduced in relation to the distinct subset sum problem. We derive a theorem outlining the optimal trade-off between two factors: the minimum cardinality of the subsets and the number of possible sums within a specified range. The complexity of this problem is shown to be essentially the same as factoring a random number of a given size in the underlying field. We apply this understanding to explain a statistical phenomenon, 'Benford's Law', by demonstrating that the distinct subset sum problem with reduced minimum cardinality significantly alters the distribution of possible sums. While this shift is mild for smaller subset sizes, the difference becomes substantial as the minimum cardinality approaches half the total size. We further develop an approximate method for solving the distinct subset sum problem by dividing the sums into ranges and using number theory to count multipliers, a technique leveraged in explaining a statistical phenomenon, 'Benoft's Law', on a range of small sums. The complexity of this approach is shown to be essentially the same as factoring a random number of a given size in the underlying field. In this study, the compass model's ability to estimate damping parameters in terms of its statistical properties is investigated. The results show that the number variance of the compass state directly impacts its ability to accurately determine damping parameters, with a minimum variance yielding the most precise estimates. Characterizing the geometry of a liquid jet is crucial for understanding its behavior, particularly when it undergoes breaking into droplets. Previous studies have primarily focused on the instabilities of liquid jets issuing from narrow conduits, leading to the development of rigorous theoretical and experimental analyses. In contrast, less is known about the behavior of wide liquid jets. Our recent x-ray free-electron laser (XFEL) experiment targeted a broad, non-breaking liquid jet, uncovering its intricate internal structure. In contrast to its breaking counterparts, this non-breaking jet exhibits a coaxial, plane-symmetric configuration, characterized by a central void surrounded by a cylindrical liquid column. An unusual, periodic density distribution is observed within the jet, attributed to the presence of air bubbles. Using computational models, we reveal that these coaxial jet configurations are stable even when subjected to minor disturbances. Additionally, we identify that the observed periodic density pattern is due to the interaction between air bubbles, which expand to fill the void at specific intervals. Our findings demonstrate the capability of XFEL-based studies to reveal the hidden details of wide liquid jets, paving the way for a deeper understanding of the intricate internal structures of breaking jets. In doing so, significant insights emerge for jet stabilization and droplet formation, which may be generalized and applied to other jet systems. Furthermore, the novel jet configurations discovered in our study could find applications in self-assembly processes, where controlled jet formations are utilized to produce desired microstructures. Our research thus offers a fresh perspective on jet geometry, opening up new avenues for further investigation and development. In the accompanying movie, we present the XFEL measurement results, along with a comparison with our numerical model predictions. The measured data, valid for a specific time, shows that the jet axis contains voids filled with X-FEL-scattered liquid, surrounded by X-FEL-scattered gases. The density of the jet appears to be highest near its surface. The movie then displays a numerical model of the jet, revealing the presence of air bubbles within its voids. As time progresses, the movie shows that the numerical model closely mimics the initial jet conditions measured by XFEL. The movie concludes by highlighting the significant differences between non-breaking and breaking jets, as well as the unique jet configurations discovered in our study. For both the deterministic and stochastic systems, we observe novel patterns of behavior that are linked to delayed nonlinearity and diffusion interactions. Specifically, increased diffusion leads to diminished effective dimensionality, while delays of a critical size can eliminate complex structures in bifurcations. In contrast, delay sizes that are multiples of a critical value can create additional periodic states. For the stochastic system, we find that a low level of diffusion can cause large, long-lasting fluctuations in the system to emerge and give rise to rare, extreme events. Conversely, very large delays can reduce the probability of these fluctuations to near zero. The denotational approach attributes meanings to entire programs rather than executions, utilizing a probabilistic type system and domain theory to define meaning through a denotational framework. The underlying probabilistic type system accounts for higher-order probabilities. This type system is similar to that proposed by Hamana and M\"ohle but incorporates them in a more comprehensive manner. The operational definition, based on a probabilistic lambda calculus, is not fully formalized here but serves as a point of reference for the denotational semantics. Instead, we examine the relationship between types and meanings within the denotational framework, focusing on the underlying denotational types and their relationship with operational types. The study reveals that denotational and operational definitions align for first-order programs but differ for higher-order programs. Specifically, denotational types define a more relaxed equality relationship, or 'almost equality', for denotational meanings. However, this equality is not always reflected in the operational definition. Nevertheless, we identify certain circumstances under which the denotational and operational definitions of meanings concur for higher-order programs. In pharmacological research, relational machine learning models are employed to draw inferences from multiple entities interacting on a graph, such as protein-ligands. Typically, models are assessed using standardized datasets and evaluation metrics derived from the original publication, but these analyses are conducted in isolation and do not provide a comprehensive understanding of the model's performance capacity. To address this limitation, we introduce a framework that facilitates comparative studies of relational models across various domains of pharmacology, utilizing a standardized benchmark dataset and extended evaluation criteria. By adopting this approach, we hope to promote more informed model selection and tailored customization of models for specific pharmacological tasks and data resources. Furthermore, we provide insights into the potential uses of derived metrics in guiding data collection efforts and informing the design of future studies. The proposed method is exemplified through analysis of 177 relational models, yielding novel conclusions about the models' performance and demonstration of the benefits of sharing data on model evaluation campaigns. The method is flexible and adaptable to various types of datasets, as evidenced by its application to prediction of protein binding constants and enzyme inhibition kinetics. Imitation learning relies on unsupervised learning to match agent and expert interactions but falls short when their environments differ. Existing approaches attempt to eliminate discrepancies by minimizing differences in input/output or both, but these fail to account for complex scenarios. Instead, we direct attention to the actual learning objective, proposing a new method for offsetting environmental variations. By leveraging the latent space captured by an encoder, we guide a decoder to reverse the effects of discrepancies on the imitation learning process. As a result, the latent representation becomes the common ground for matching expert and agent behaviors. During training, the decoder is optimized to map common ground to shared outputs and, through backpropagation, the encoder is updated to minimize conceptual differences. This method performs consistently or better than current baselines across a range of imitation challenges. Moreover, it facilitates transferring learned behaviors across varying environments without requiring explicit domain adaptation steps. Ultimately, the method allows Imitation Learning to effectively account for environmental variations and efficiently transfer knowledge to similar domains. The code is publicly available on https://github.com/alecard/dvae. A measurement map, $m$, is generated through multiple measurements, each capturing the radio signal strength at specific locations. A radio map, $r$, is then derived from $m$ via a smoothing process. We define a map uncertainty metric as the expected distance between a measured map, $m_i$, and a normalized version of the map, $r$, and show that this metric can be minimized through an optimal allocation of resources for map estimation. We formulate the solution to this problem as a non-convex optimization problem, and derive both lower and upper bounds for the optimal solution. We then propose a distributed solution that achieves the lower bound, and validate the effectiveness of this approach through simulations and a pilot experimental implementation. Our investigation focused on a specific task - identifying and categorizing vehicle make and model information from images, a problem that necessitates a comprehensive understanding of vehicle geometry and the relationship between vehicle make and model. We provide insight into their effectiveness and possible applications on smaller datasets, and suggest further research is needed to fully utilize their potential. We investigate the estimate of a function of several parameters in a parametric model, where the function is expressed as a sum of unknown statistical elements. Under certain conditions, we demonstrate that weak convergence of the estimate function arises from the asymptotic behavior of the estimates of individual statistical elements, as their sample sizes approach infinity. Our results are applicable to multiple statistical models, including the mixture of normals, latent class, and change-point models, where identifying the individual statistical elements is a key challenge. We present specific applications of our theory, along with a new method for estimating the parameters of a function in these models, which often yields improved accuracy over conventional estimates. Numerical experiments support our theoretical findings, and we also present two real-world data sets as examples. Our approach shares similarities with the component analysis technique, but differs in its underlying mathematical framework. Moreover, we show that the estimates obtained using our method are often based on sparse distributions across the various statistical elements. Although our method is inspired by Bayesian approaches, its results can be interpreted in a frequentist context. Our work is worthy of note, as it provides novel frequentist interpretations of multiple complex statistical models. These interpretations are particularly significant for mixture of normals, change-point, and functional linear regression models. Our method is implemented in the R package named funcepi. 

Here are the numerical results:
- Our method outperformed the current best frequentist approaches for estimating parameters in mixture of normals and change-point models.
- It compared favorably to Bayesian methods, particularly those featuring the SWAG precursor to the VITROBY sampler.
- It demonstrated superior performance on a real-world data set for the segment identification sub-problem in the fitting of regression splines. 

Ultimately, our research highlighted the potential for weakly convergent estimates of function estimates, provided that individual statistical elements meet certain asymptotic criteria. This principle can be extended to obtain the weak convergence of estimate distributions, given that the estimates of individual statistical elements themselves converge weakly.

In our research, we explore the existence of equilibrium in mean field games involving continuous-time dynamics and affine controls, subject to regularity constraints. However, even under relatively mild assumptions, we find that the requirement for regularity significantly impedes the existence of equilibrium compared to games without such constraints. To illustrate this phenomenon, we establish the existence of equilibrium in a specific class of mean field games featuring continuous time dynamics and Lagrange multiplier based regularity, as well as games involving a unique constant coefficient Hamiltonian. Moreover, we demonstrate the absence of equilibrium in a particular class of mean field games involving time-dependent Hamiltonian dynamics without any form of regularity. Ultimately, our research reveals the critical role that regularity plays in determining the existence of equilibrium in mean field games. Detecting outfit discrepancies has significant practical value, as it enables retailers to prevent counterfeit clothing and clothing swap scams with precise accuracy. Current methods are limited due to the complexity of accurate discrepancy identification, which poses significant technical challenges. We propose an innovative approach, OutfitDiff, which leverages cutting-edge fashion outfit recognition models to analyze both outfit and discrepancy images, while incorporating style and semantic alignment via a Style Semantic Alignment Network (SSAN). Non-classical resource theories are playing a significant role in promoting new quantum information protocols. They have led to the development of methodologies, the proof of beliefs, and hopes regarding the utility of such resources. However, there is an absence of a unified approach to studying non-classical resource theories, which are based on specific measurement outcomes. This lack of structure prevents the comparison of such theories and their associated resources. To address this challenge, we introduce a basic framework to study non-classical resource theories based on specific measurement outcomes. Using this framework, we re-examine the resource theories of entanglement, quantum coherence, and continuous-variable multipartite entanglement. Our analysis involves identifying non-classical resources, demonstrating their utility in enhancing various tasks, and providing a clear comparison of these resource theories. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the resource theories and their associated interpolation problems, which are crucial for quantifying the resources available in such theories. Our study paves the way for the creation of a database where various non-classical resource theories and their associated resources can be compared and shared. This resource, called necs.nist.gov/nrt/, is now accessible. To enhance the scalability of federated learning while maintaining data privacy, we introduce FedBuff, a novel framework that capitalizes on exponential moving average. FedBuff's efficient use of a single global buffer enables per-client updates via weighted linear transformations, significantly reducing communication overhead by minimizing the number of messages exchanged. The buffer's weighted average acts as a makeshift aggregated gradient, allowing FedBuff to mimic the behavior of vanilla federated learning, especially when the learning rate is appropriately set. Furthermore, FedBuff's performance converges to that of vanilla federated learning as the learning rate diminishes. We validate the efficacy of FedBuff through comprehensive experiments, which demonstrate its comparable convergence to MOA and faster convergence than ADF, while also highlighting its potential to replace ADAM, a popular stochastic gradient descent method. The source code for FedBuff is publicly available on GitHub at the specified link. \href{https://github.com/hpqr20/FedBuff}{https://github.com/hpqr20/FedBuff}. Keywords: Federated Learning, Exponential Moving Average, Scalability, Efficiency, Federated Adaptive Gradient.

When compared to standalone GaN, using ZnGeN$_2$ leads to a 40% increase in room-temperature hole mobility, while using MgSiN$_2$ yields a 165 times increase.  Through simulation, the team determined that while both materials reduce defects in GaN, ZnGeN$_2$'s larger GeN$_2$ holes are more effective at minimizing impact, thereby increasing mobility.  These findings support the use of solid solutions of GaN and MgSiN$_2$ (derived from ZnGeN$_2$ and MgSiN$_2$) as optimal materials for improving GaN's hole mobility.  Ultimately, these novel nitrides can be used to enhance the efficiency of GaN-based power electronic devices.  The team's research provides a new approach for developing more efficient solid-state power amplifiers and reducing energy losses in GaN and microelectromechanical systems. The concept of temporal knowledge graphs is a time-sensitive expansion on traditional knowledge graphs, representing real-world events through their timestamped associations. Consequently, there's a significant need for creating high-accuracy temporal knowledge graph embeddings that capture both node properties and timeline developments. This study focuses on the relationships between insplits and outsplits of matrices, particularly graph matrices, to understand their equivalence under certain conditions. It is found that certain criteria can determine when two insplits or outsplits are equivalent, and these findings are extended to the concept of strong shift equivalence. It is demonstrated that strong shift equivalence can be defined by a different set of insplits and outsplits, and this characterization is significant because it is based on a fundamental property of matrices that is independent of the matrix size or rank. In addition, the study explores connections between insplits, outsplits, and minimal strong shift equivalences, particularly in the context of unitary matrices. An important question remains unanswered: can every strong shift equivalence be defined by a set of insplits and outsplits that satisfy a specific condition? To address this, a reduced form of the question is posed by defining a new set of equivalences. This work is significant because it sheds light on the relationships between insplits, outsplits, and graph matrices, particularly in the context of unitary matrices. The study also identifies new candidates for minimal strong shift equivalences and provides a new characterization of strong shift equivalences based on insplits and outsplits. Ultimately, the research aims to contribute to a broader understanding of graph theory and the relationships between various mathematical objects. The examples demonstrate that certain properties can determine the equivalence of insplits or outsplits, and these properties are shown to apply to a wide range of mathematical objects, including graphs and star shapes. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the relationships between insplits, outsplits, and graph matrices are connected to the concepts of contractibility, weak shift equivalence, and graph contraction. structural information from knowledge graphs to enhance its understanding of
language. By incorporating a Knowledge interaction layer, OREO-LLM models like
Transformers and CNNs can tap into this structural information, facilitating more

responsible for this improvement. As a result, OREO-LM presents a viable option

Recent research on large language models has shown the potential for adaptability and generalization beyond control tasks. Non-critical, task-agnostic prompts not used for pre-training can significantly impact model performance. Since prompts used during adaptation may contain novel words, a challenge arises regarding their processing. Our study presents a prompt processing method called CogSLP, which enables self-supervised learning of sentence representations from diverse prompts. CogSLP is evaluated through zero-shot language understanding tasks and comparisons with other relevant approaches. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of CogSLP in processing novel prompts and improving model performance. Moreover, analyses reveal CogSLP's ability to learn semantic representations that are less sensitive to prompt variations. This research may have implications for developing prompt-conditioned generative models and exploring the semantic aspect of prompt conditioning. Moreover, our findings may shed light on the potential of self-supervised learning of sentence representations in simulating natural conversation. To enhance the precision of Rydberg atom-based measurements under noisy conditions, we integrate a deep learning approach with a quantum algorithm. By training a neural network using imprecise Rydberg interactions, its ability to distinguish a range of entanglement levels is demonstrated. We show that the deep learning technique effectively extracts information about multiple qubits through multiple two-qubit interactions, without resolving individual qubit states. This approach is particularly effective in noisy environments, outperforming a conventional quantum algorithm without using a neural network. Additionally, we find that the neural network can distinguish multiple qubits more accurately when interactions between fewer qubits are involved. However, this increased resolution comes at a cost of reducing the measurable range of entanglement levels. Nonetheless, our results indicate a promising future for integrating deep learning with quantum algorithms to enhance precision measurements in complex systems. Moreover, this research paves the way for using Rydberg atoms not just as precision measuring instruments, but also as multi-qubit quantum systems. Finally, we speculate that the neural network's ability to distinguish multiple qubits could be achieved by analyzing fluctuations in the amplitude of its outputs. Therefore, by exploring the underlying structure of the Rydberg Hamiltonian, we hope to establish a theoretical framework for the neural network's behavior. Such a understanding could also be applied to other similar systems where complex quantum dynamics occur. Furthermore, our study demonstrates the potential of using artificial intelligence to study complex quantum systems where identifying individual events is difficult. Conversely, we also examine how the precision measuring capabilities of Rydberg atoms could be used to improve neural network classifications by exploiting the unique properties of these atoms. By integrating artificial intelligence with quantum algorithms, we can reach new heights of precision and computation, thus unleashing new innovative applications at the intersection of quantum information and artificial intelligence. \textbf{Our code can be accessed at https://github.com/asherouse/NN_Rydberg\_Hamiltonian.}

We analyze the Julia set of a quasiregular map from $\mathbb{R}^n$ to itself, focusing on how its Hausdorff dimension is related to the properties of its image under iterates. Our findings hold whether or not the map has a fixed point or is a hyperbolic function. By contrast, the study of Julia sets in conformal maps is a more established field. A key difference between our work and prior research is that we do not assume our quasiregular maps are locally non-archimedean, which is essential for applying other known results. Instead, we prove that for any quasiregular map, its Julia set has a dimension less than or equal to the product of its topological dimension and the exponent of its Liouvillé function. This achievement is a consequence of our investigation into the properties of Julia sets in the context of quasiregular maps. A significant outcome of our research is that the Julia set of a quasiregular map with a fixed point or a hyperbolic component has a Hausdorff dimension of zero, unless it is identical to the entire space. We show that the boundary of the preimage of a small ball under iterates of a quasiregular map is roughly equivalent in size to the ball itself, which contributes to our overall results. Our study also reveals that the Julia set of a quasiregular map is precisely the set of points whose forward images under iterates have positive Hausdorff dimension. A crucial tool in supporting our findings is that the forward images of a quasiregular map are essentially equivalent in size and dimension to their preimages, which is a key dimension-related result. Initially, focus is directed towards the exclusive decays of several heavy vector mesons, including ρ mesons and J/ψ, ψ(2S), and ϒ. The findings indicate that heavy vector mesons are preferentially produced at large rapidities through a quark-dominated process. Semi-inclusive measurements, involving the detection of charged pions in conjunction with various heavy vector mesons, provide additional insight. By accounting for detection biases, it is found that the inclusive and semi-inclusive cross-section measurements align well. Despite their effectiveness, Fully Connected Recurrent Neural Networks (FCRNNs) face significant challenges during training due to their inefficient parallel computation and substantial memory demands. To overcome these limitations, researchers have explored alternative architectures such as Local RNNs, which involve removing horizontal connections to reduce memory requirements and facilitate efficient parallel training. However, this modification comes with a cost, primarily affecting the model's performance. In an effort to strike a balance between training efficiency and performance, we introduce a new method called Sample Permutation, which enables the parallel training of FCRNNs through the swapping of input samples. We test this method on diverse RNN variants and performance metrics, and our experiments demonstrate that it can yield performance gains equivalent to those achieved by Local RNNs, all while reducing the model size by a substantial margin. In addition to its applications during training, we show that our method can also function as an effective data augmentation technique during inference. In an effort to facilitate the adoption of our method, we have developed an open-source implementation, known as Permutation RNN, which includes a range of pre-trained models. These pre-trained models have applications in a variety of tasks including stock market forecasting, seismology, and robotics. In order to facilitate the replication of our results, we have made available both our implementation and the numerical data used to validate our method. Past research on epidemiological models often employed the REQA framework, although it struggles to account for critical phenomena, such as vaccine efficacy and viral mutation. To address these limitations, we developed MARE, a modular and flexible object-oriented model which leverages fundamental mathematical concepts to effectively represent various aspects of SARS-CoV-2 transmission. By pacing model evolution according to real-world time, MARE effectively tackles the triple trade-off of aligning medical success with both economic gains and social welfare. Through numerical experiments, MARE consistently emerged as a suitable candidate for expert policy advice, even when compared to widely used models within the REQA framework. To facilitate seamless collaboration among experts from diverse modeling backgrounds, MARE offers a range of built-in models, accommodating different assumptions and levels of complexity. Debugging data-intensive machine learning (MLE) pipelines poses an insurmountable challenge for current data debugging tools, largely due to their limitation in handling multi-stage data pipelines. These tools typically produce vague error messages, forcing developers to engage in extensive, time-consuming processes involving data inspection and pipeline reconfiguration. Furthermore, they often fail to provide any measurable improvement in pipeline execution speed. In response to these shortcomings, we introduce DataScope, a innovative data debugging tool designed for handling complex MLE pipelines. DataScope's key contributions stem from its ability to (a) accurately pinpoint problems in pipelines through in-depth data analysis, (b) modify data on-the-fly to facilitate rapid prototyping, and (c) streamline pipeline processing with a high-performance pipeline reconfiguration technique. In our experiments, DataScope has demonstrated remarkable capabilities, including a 50x pipeline speedup and a 100x reduction in data processing time for pipeline reconfiguration. Our benchmark results have also shown DataScope's notable superiority over other leading data debugging tools, with a 10x improvement in efficiency. In addition, DataScope has successfully resolved issues in real-world MLE pipeline scenarios, as demonstrated in our practical study involving data ingestion pipeline failures. In summary, DataScope represents a cutting-edge data debugging solution, empowering developers to create high-quality MLE pipelines with enhanced data quality and reduced development time.
